Alright, do you know what’s happening this weekend? I’ve got a thing about Shakespeare week, and we’re going to Stratford-upon-Avon. It’s going to be a real treat. Oh, really? I love Shakespeare! I mean, I love the stories, but I also love the fact that there’s a real circus workshop happening in Stratford. I heard about it on the radio. They’ve got a real circus, not one of those boring ones with just a few acts. Yeah! I want to see the real circus! I heard they’ve got acrobats and jugglers and even a magician who does stop motion animation with toys. It’s like magic, but with moving pictures! Oh, you’re going to love that. And there’s also the pirates theme for Easter, which is going to be the biggest thing in the town. They’ve got pirate ships and treasure hunts and even a pirate-themed picture day. You know, like a photo session with the pirates. That’s sounds so fun. I’m going to wear a pirate hat and a scarf and try to look like a real pirate. Maybe even get a picture with a sword and a parrot. I want a parrot! I saw one on the way to school yesterday – it was talking to the ducks, and it said, “Quack, quack, quack!” It was silly and funny. Ha! That sounds exactly like something a pirate would do. Oh, and also, they’re doing a magic show in the local park. They said it’s all kid-friendly and has tricks with cards and coins. You can even make your own magic tricks at the end. That sounds cool. I wish we had magic shows back home. I’ve only seen one once when I was at my nan’s. She had a little magic box with cards, and she made the cards disappear. It was amazing. I want to learn magic! I want to make coins disappear and make things float. I heard that there’s a stop motion animation workshop happening next week as well. Maybe they’ll let me try it. That’s the best part – you can try everything. You can learn magic, you can make your own stop motion videos, you can even meet real pirates. It’s going to be the most fun week of the year. I can’t wait.

So, do you remember that time we were in Saudi Arabia, Bill? I was teaching English, and one day I got a call from the police. They said I was wanted for something... I think it had to do with a boat. Oh, you mean the infamous  Deerhound ? That was a  real  doozie. You tried to sail from Jeddah to Cyprus, didn’t you? Yeah, I remember that. You were so sure you could just slip out of the country in a boat and nobody would chase you. But the Saudi authorities don’t take kindly to smuggling, even if it’s just a tiny dinghy. I think they caught you before you even got out of the port. The police showed up at the marina, and you were trying to load the boat with some goods. They said you were breaking the law, and they arrested you on the spot. Exactly! And they didn’t even let me explain that I was just looking for a bit of adventure. I was teaching English, not smuggling! I bet they thought you were up to no good. But you were a bit of a legend, you know. The locals would talk about you for weeks. “That English teacher who tried to sail away from Jeddah with a boat full of... whatever.” It was a bizarre thing. You were sentenced to a few months in a detention center, and then you just wandered back to the UK on a plane. You had a bit of a celebrity status in the expat community for a while. Oh, I was  so  popular. Everyone wanted to hear about how I got arrested for trying to sail from Saudi Arabia. It was like being a movie star. I bet you were the first teacher to do that. I remember reading about it in the  Times  back then. They called it the “sailor teacher scandal.” I had a bit of a reputation for that. I told all the students about it, and they laughed. It was like a story that never ended. Speaking of stories, there was that time you tried to sell some dental magazines in the market. You said it was a business idea. Yeah, you started off with a few magazines, thinking you’d make a quick buck. But the market in Riyadh wasn’t exactly the best place to sell dental magazines. And then, of course, you ended up with a crowd of people around you, arguing over the price.

So, do you think he’s ready for the new school year? I mean, he’s been acting so strangely lately. Yeah, I’m not sure. He’s been disappearing into his room a lot, and when I ask him what’s going on, he just shrugs and says, “Nothing.” It’s like he’s got something on his mind but won’t talk about it. Maybe he’s just stressed about starting again. I mean, he’s moving to a new school, isn’t he? That’s a big change for a kid. Yeah, he’s got a lot to adjust to. I mean, he’s moving from a small town to a bigger city, and now he’s got a new group of friends. It’s not easy for someone his age. I can imagine. I remember when I was his age, moving was a big deal. I had to leave my old friends and start fresh. It’s hard on the emotional side, even if it’s exciting. Yeah, I guess. But I don’t want him to feel like he’s being left out. I’ve been thinking about getting him a part-time job to help him settle in. Maybe something like babysitting or refereeing? He’s been asking about work experience a lot lately. That’s a good idea. He’s got a good attitude and is pretty responsible. I know he’s been trying to get some work experience through the school, but they’re pretty limited. Maybe there are some opportunities in the area. I know a few people who run a football club near the town. They’re always looking for referees, especially for younger kids. Maybe we can put him in touch with them. That sounds cool. I mean, he loves sports, and refereeing is a good way for him to get out there and meet people. Plus, it’s a chance to earn some pocket money while he’s figuring things out. Yeah, and it gives him something to focus on. It’s not like he’s just sitting around doing nothing. I mean, being a teenager is tough, but having a bit of structure helps. Absolutely. And if he’s got a bit of money, maybe he can even go on a holiday with his mates. I mean, he’s been talking about going on a camping trip with his friends in the summer.

I can't believe we've got truffles in Croatia, dad. I thought they were like, only in Italy or France or something. Well, truffles are pretty much everywhere now, especially with the foodie movement. You can even find them in places you'd never expect. And I think it's because of chefs like Massimo Bottura or Gordon Ramsay—they’ve brought truffle culture into the mainstream. Yeah, but truffles are so expensive. I mean, how do people even afford to eat them? Oh, they don't eat them every day. It's more like a luxury, a special treat. Like how some people might buy a steak only once a month. And besides, you don't need to eat truffles to enjoy good food. There's so much more to cooking than just that one ingredient. I guess, but truffles are amazing. I mean, just the smell alone is intoxicating. I remember in America, my friend’s mom used to have truffle oil on everything. It was like,  this is fancy . Yeah, but I think Americans tend to overdo it with the truffle oil. It’s like, everything has to be super fancy. But I love how it adds that umami flavor. It’s like the king of aromatics. Wait, what’s umami? It’s like the fifth taste—along with sweet, salty, sour, and bitter. It’s that deep, savory flavor you get from things like mushrooms, tomatoes, and yes, truffles. It’s what makes food taste rich and delicious. Oh, I hadn’t heard of that before. I mean, I know about the other ones, but umami is new to me. I guess that’s why chefs are always telling you to cook with it. It makes everything more complex. Exactly. And if you’re cooking at home, you don’t have to go overboard. A little bit of truffle oil, or even truffle salt, can elevate a simple dish. Like, I once made a simple tomato pasta with some truffle salt and it was incredible. That sounds fancy. But I don’t know if I’d want to try it. I mean, it’s like,  I don’t know if I like the taste of that . Well, it’s your choice. But I think you’d be surprised. It’s not like it’s going to taste like something you don’t like. It just adds a different dimension.

So, do you know what’s going on with the new project? I’ve been trying to get some clarity on it, but it’s all a bit of a blur. Yeah, I heard there's some major changes with the digital platform. I think they’re overhauling the entire system. It’s all about integrating more AI into the publishing process. Oh, really? I thought they were just updating the website. I mean, I’ve been working on the projects assistant role, and I’ve seen a few changes, but nothing too drastic. Just more automated tools for the editorial team. That’s what I thought too. But I overheard the head of publishing talking about something bigger. It’s like they’re planning to make the platform more interactive, maybe even more like a social media space for authors and readers. That’s an interesting idea, but I can see the challenges. You can’t just turn a publishing house into a social media platform overnight. It would take time and a lot of planning. Yeah, I guess so. I mean, it’s not like we’re not already using some digital tools. We have a content management system, and the editorial team uses some AI tools for grammar checks and basic content analysis. Maybe they want to take it further? Exactly. I think they want to stay competitive in the digital age. With the way people consume content now, it’s not just about books anymore. It’s about experiences, engagement, and community. I’ve been reading about a lot of publishers doing similar things. Some are even experimenting with augmented reality in their books. It’s all part of the shift to make reading more immersive and personalized. That does sound exciting, but I’m not sure how it would work in practice. I mean, we’re still dealing with the basics—getting manuscripts in on time, managing deadlines, and ensuring quality. If they add more layers to the process, it might slow things down. That’s a valid point. It’s a balance between innovation and efficiency. I think as long as they don’t lose sight of their core mission, it could work. But I’m also curious about the implications for authors and the publishing process itself. Definitely. It’s a big change, and it’s going to affect everyone involved. I wonder if they’re planning any training sessions or workshops for the team to get up to speed with the new tools.

So, do you think we’ll make it in time for the party? I know it’s only a short drive, but the roads can be a bit unpredictable at this time of day. I hope so. I left the house about an hour ago, and the motorway’s been pretty clear. I think we’ll be fine. Though I was worried about the toll booths—still don’t know why they’re so strict in Poland. I remember reading something about how they’re trying to introduce more electronic toll systems. It’s a bit of a hassle when you’re used to just waving through. Yeah, I’ve had a few problems with that. I once got stuck in a queue for like 20 minutes just because my card wasn’t properly registered. I had to pull over, get out, and hand it to the guy. It was ridiculous. That must have been frustrating. I guess it’s just a bit of a cultural thing, isn’t it? You never know what to expect when you’re driving in a foreign country. Definitely. I mean, we’ve been through so many different places, and every country has its own quirks. I think the best way to handle it is just to stay calm and not get too stressed about the small things. Yeah, I agree. It’s the same as when I used to travel for work. You learn to roll with the punches. Though, honestly, I’m just glad we’re not driving in the opposite direction. I wouldn’t have liked that. Oh, I know. I was really stressed when I first started driving here. I kept thinking, “What if I miss a turn? What if I get lost?” But it’s actually not that bad once you get the hang of it. That’s reassuring. I still have that fear of getting lost, though. I always carry a map just in case. You could always use the GPS. I don’t know how people manage without it. I mean, it’s not perfect, but it’s better than trying to read a paper map while you’re trying to keep the car on the road. I guess so. I’ve been trying to get better at using it. I think I’ve finally got the hang of it. Though I still get confused with all the different names of the roads.

I can't believe the new Tottenham kit. It's so bold. I mean, it's not even close to the old design. I think they went for something more modern, but honestly, it looks a bit too flashy for my taste. I know, right? I was watching it on the TV earlier, and I couldn't help but think they’re trying too hard. But I guess that’s the thing with sports sponsorship these days. If you’re not making a statement, you’re not getting noticed. Yeah, and with the way sponsors are pushing for visibility, I guess it's hard to ignore. But I still think they could have balanced it a bit more. The red and white are great, but that black and gold around the sleeves? It feels like it's trying to be too much. I get what you mean. I think they’re making a statement about the club’s identity, but it’s a bit confusing. Like, they’re trying to be edgy, but the design doesn’t quite follow through. I mean, isn't that the whole point of a kit? To represent the team’s history and identity, not just make a fashion statement. Exactly. I think it's a shame they didn't stick with something more traditional. But then again, I guess football is changing. I mean, I can still remember when the kits were much simpler. You didn’t need to wear a sponsor’s logo on the back or have crazy patterns on your socks. True. But then again, the way the game is now, with all the money involved, they’re not just playing for pride anymore. They’re playing for sponsors, for branding, for visibility. It’s all about selling the image of the club as much as the game itself. I guess that's the price of being part of the Premier League. But it does make me wonder if the fans are even interested in the actual design anymore. I mean, when you're just watching the game on TV, you probably don’t even notice the kit unless it’s a big story or something. Yeah, but sometimes the kits become a talking point on their own. Like with the recent McDonald’s sponsorship. I mean, I get it, they're trying to get their brand out there, but I think it's a bit of a gimmick.

I just got a message from my cousin, and she’s mad at me again. She said I didn’t even call her to check in on how her kids are doing after that day trip we were supposed to take together. You know how she is—always expecting you to be on call. She’s got that whole  I’ve got kids, you’ve got to be there for them  thing going on. Yeah, but this isn’t even about that. It’s about the fact that I’ve been trying to get back into the job market, and she’s still insisting I should just take the job seeker’s allowance and  not  throw myself into the system. You know what? I’ve been there, you know. When I was unemployed for over two years, I thought the same thing—why bother? It’s like the system doesn’t even want to help you. Exactly. I mean, I’ve got a degree, and I’m not even being considered for anything. It’s like the employers just want people with no experience—so they can train them from scratch. I know, it’s so frustrating. I tried applying for a few things, but they all ask for references, and I don’t even have one. I mean, I used to work in retail, but now it’s like nobody wants to hire someone who’s been out of work for so long. And don’t even get me started on the gas and electricity bills. I’m living in my parents’ house, and I can’t even afford to cook properly. I just heat up some instant noodles and hope for the best. I know, I know. I’ve been trying to cook on the George Foreman grill, and it’s like trying to cook in a sauna. I’ve burnt more food than I’ve cooked. You know what’s even worse? My brother-in-law. He’s got a huge inheritance, and he’s just wasting it on fancy cars and stuff. You’d think he’d be helping out his family instead of being out there buying stuff he doesn’t need. I’ve seen it. He’s got a brand new Range Rover, and the kids are still in the same old second-hand cars. It’s like he doesn’t even care about the family.

So, do you think we should get some cake for the afternoon? I’ve been thinking it would be nice to have something sweet after our coffee. Oh, I’d love that. But are we getting it from the local shop or one of those big chains? I mean, the convenience store down the road has nice treats, but I’m not sure about the quality. Oh, don’t you worry, love. I know a few places that make the best cakes. The ones in the village, actually. You can get proper fresh ones there. Didn’t you say you used to go there when you were younger? Yeah, I used to. But I haven’t been in years. I think the shop’s been there forever, though. Maybe it’s still the same. I suppose, but these days, I think they’ve started selling more of that branded stuff. The ones that come in boxes. I mean, they’re alright for a quick snack, but not the same as a homemade cake. That’s why I like going to the shop with the old lady who runs it. She used to make these shortbread tarts that were to die for. I’d take her a bag of tea every week, and she’d give me a tart in return. Made my day every time. That sounds lovely. I used to like that sort of thing too. It’s the kind of place where you could just pop in and chat, and the people knew your name. These days, it’s all about speed and efficiency, isn’t it? Yeah, I know. I think the younger generation just wants everything fast. But I miss the days when people actually knew each other. I mean, even the traffic here is different now. I used to be able to navigate without a sat nav. Now I’m like, “Where am I? Why is this road called this?” Oh, I know. I used to drive to the city all the time, and I relied on the radio for directions. You’d get a gist of where you were going, and if you didn’t, you’d just figure it out. These days, you’re supposed to know where you are, even if you’re miles from the city. I think it’s more about not wanting to be lost. I mean, I’m not a fan of the sat nav either.

So, do you know what’s happening with the new trainee teachers at the school? No, what’s going on? I heard they’re all really strict, like, super strict. I think one of them even got into a fight with the headteacher last week. Oh no, really? That’s not good. Yeah, I mean, I don’t know if it’s true, but I heard someone say she was shouting at the students and then the headteacher stepped in and told her to calm down. Wow, that sounds intense. I hope they don’t get fired. Yeah, I guess that’s a bit harsh, but I mean, they’re new, right? They probably don’t know how to handle the class yet. Maybe they just need a bit of time. I mean, I’ve got this new English teacher this term, and she’s not too bad. She’s got this really cool way of making us laugh during lessons. Oh yeah, I remember her from last year. I think she used to teach science. Yeah, and then she got promoted to English. I guess it’s a good move. She’s really passionate about it. I wish our science teacher was like that. He’s so boring. We just do the same thing every lesson. I know, right? I think he just wants to get through the day without any trouble. Yeah, and the art teacher is the opposite. She’s always coming up with wild ideas and she lets us do whatever we want. That’s the best part of art class. I can just draw whatever I want without worrying about rules. I mean, I like it, but sometimes I feel like it’s not helping me with exams. Yeah, I get that. I think it’s hard to balance creativity with the stuff we need to learn for tests. I heard that the English test is coming up soon. Are you nervous? A bit, honestly. I’m not sure I’ve studied enough. Me too. I think I’m going to start revising tomorrow. Maybe I’ll make a study schedule or something. That sounds like a good idea. I might do that too. And what about the science test? I feel like I’m completely lost. I know, I’ve been trying to memorize all the formulas, but it’s so confusing. Maybe we can study together?

Alright, do you know what’s the biggest thing I’ve learned since I’ve been home with the toddler? It’s that the world is full of people who think they know everything, but actually, they don’t. Yeah, I know what you mean. Like, my teacher at school was saying that religion is the biggest source of conflict in the world, but I think it depends on how you look at it. Exactly! I mean, I don’t think religion is the problem. It’s just that people take it too seriously. Like, when I was in school, they told us that nuns are all very holy and they do good things, but now I think some of them are just stressed and they get annoyed with the kids. Yeah, like, I saw a video online about a nun who got really angry at a kid for spilling juice on the floor. And she yelled at him like, “You’re going to hell!” I thought that was kind of over the top. Oh, I’ve seen that too. And I think some of the nuns do things that are kind of weird. Like, I heard that some of them wear black and they don’t even smile. I think they’re like, “We’re not supposed to have fun.” Wait, but isn’t that part of their religion? Like, if you’re a nun, you’re supposed to be serious and not laugh too much? Maybe, but I think some of them just don’t like being smiled at. I mean, they’ve been doing it for years, and now they’re just like, “We don’t want to smile anymore.” Mmm mmm. Oh, there you go. That’s your way of saying you’re hungry, isn’t it? Yeah, he must be. I think he’s ready for dessert. But I was just thinking about something else – have you ever watched the Matrix? I saw it on YouTube, and it’s like, “Everything is a simulation.” Oh, I’ve heard about that. I think it’s like, the world you’re living in is not real. Like, you’re just in a machine, and you’re being fed information. Yeah, and I think that’s what some people believe about religion too. Like, some people think that all the things we believe in are just a simulation, and we’re just pretending to be religious.

So, do you think I should actually go to those dancing lessons? I mean, I’ve been meaning to get back into it, but I’m not sure if I’m ready. Honestly, I think it’s never too late to try. I mean, you’ve got the energy, and if it’s something you enjoy, why not? It’s not like you’re going to be bad at it — I’ve seen you dance at family gatherings before! Yeah, but I’m not sure if I’m the type to just pick it up and be good at it. I mean, I’ve always been like, “I can do this, I can do that,” but then I end up not actually doing it. That’s the thing though — it’s not about being perfect. It’s about having fun and getting out of your comfort zone. You know, I was thinking the other day about how when I was in university, I used to hate doing group work, but now I’m actually getting into collaborating on projects. It’s just about giving it a go. I guess that’s true. But I’m also thinking about the holidays — like, if I go to those lessons, am I going to have time to actually enjoy my holiday? I mean, I got booked on a trip to York for next month, and I don’t want to be busy with something else. You know what? Maybe you could do both. You don’t have to dedicate all your time to dancing — just an hour a week or something. And if you like it, you can keep going. But if you don’t, you can always stop. It’s not like you’re committing to anything serious. I guess that does make sense. I just worry about being judged or feeling like I’m not good enough. I mean, I’ve always been a bit of a fussy eater, so I guess I’m kind of a fussy person in general. I want to do things the right way. That’s relatable. I mean, I always wanted to learn to play the piano when I was younger, but I always thought I wasn’t “talented” enough. But then, when I actually started, I realized it wasn’t about talent — it was about practice and persistence. I wonder if that’s how it works with dancing too.

So, do you think we should stop for lunch soon? I’m starving. Yeah, I think we should. The last place we passed had a nice little café, and I saw a sign saying it serves good local olive oil and wine. Can we stop at the market too? I saw a sign for a farmers’ market just a few miles ahead. That’s a good idea. I love markets—especially here in Istria. Absolutely. I’ve also heard the wine is amazing. Maybe we can pick up a bottle for the evening. I think there’s a place with a nice view by the lake. That sounds perfect. I’d love a drive through the countryside with some good wine and a view. Can we also stop at that campsite I saw? It looked really peaceful. I’d like to set up the caravan and just stay for a while. That might be tricky, though. We’re already on a tight schedule. We want to see as much as we can before we head back. I get that, but maybe we can just check it out for a bit. It might be a nice spot to rest for the night. Let me check my map. It says there’s a campsite with a lake nearby. I think it’s called the Istrian Lakes Campsite. I’ve heard it’s a great place to stay. Cool! I can bring my phone charger and some snacks. Maybe we can also check out the restaurant nearby. I heard it’s really good. That’s a good plan. I’d like to try some local food too. I’ve heard they serve grilled fish with herbs and olive oil. I could eat that every day. I love seafood. And while we’re in the area, do you think we should plan our route for tomorrow? I’d like to make sure we don’t go off track. Yeah, maybe. I’m excited to see the rest of the region. I’ve heard there are some beautiful parks and art installations. I also want to see the rock formations near the coast. I’m not sure if we’ll have time, though.

So, do you know what’s up with the whole recording thing? I saw this video of someone doing something really... intense and it was just so weird. I couldn’t even watch it all the way through. Oh, you mean that one where they were like...  snaps fingers ... yeah, the one where they were doing that with the camera and everything? I think it was like a game or something? Yeah, that was the one. I remember my cousin watched it, and she said she was so confused. Like, why would you do that? It just looked so... uncomfortable. I don’t even know. I think some people just like to push boundaries, you know? My friend Tash did that once. She got so into it that she started recording her own stuff, even though I told her not to. She said it was just for fun. Yeah, but I mean, isn’t it kind of weird? Like, what’s the point of showing that? I mean, I get that people want to be seen, but like... I don’t know. It just feels too much. I guess it’s different for everyone. For some people, it’s just a way to feel powerful or in control. Like, “I’m doing this, and I’m not afraid of being judged.” But for others, it’s like... not cool at all. I think it’s also about the culture. Like, some people just grew up in an environment where that’s normal. I mean, I’ve seen some of my friends’ families do weird things like that, and they just think it’s regular. Yeah, and I think with the internet and social media, it’s just easier to get away with it. You can post anything and no one really knows. It’s like, “Oh, I did that, and no one cares.” But then again, what if someone  does  care? I mean, if you’re doing something like that, there’s always the possibility that someone could get hurt or feel uncomfortable. You can’t really control how people take it. That’s true. I mean, even if you think it’s just a game, sometimes it can cross the line. I remember hearing about a few cases where people got in trouble for doing that kind of stuff without thinking about the consequences. Yeah, and you don’t even know who’s watching.

So, do you know where the best coffee in this place is? I’ve been here a few times, but I’m still not sure if I’m getting the best brew. Honestly, I think the café in the basement is alright, but I’ve heard people say the one in the main library is better. I tried it once, but it was so busy I couldn’t even get a seat. Yeah, I think that’s the one. I’ve heard the baristas there are pretty good. They do a decent cappuccino and the pastries are actually worth the extra pound. That’s what I thought too. I mean, we’re paying for the university, so we might as well get a decent cup of coffee. Although, I’m not sure if I’m ready for the price jump from the vending machines to the real thing. Oh, you’re not alone. I’ve been trying to cut down on my coffee addiction, but when the baristas are so friendly and the coffee smells so good, it’s hard to resist. I know what you mean. I used to drink way too much of that strong black stuff from the vending machine. It was like drinking motor oil. I’ve been trying to switch to something a bit more palatable. I’ve actually been looking into some of the local cafés too. I heard there’s a new place just a few streets away that uses ethically sourced beans. I’m curious to try it out. That sounds promising. I’ll have to check it out. I’m not sure if I’m ready to leave the library just yet, but if the coffee is any good, I might have to make an exception. Yeah, the library is a bit of a sanctuary for us. It’s peaceful, and you can actually get some work done without the distractions of the café. True, but sometimes I think the coffee here is just a bit too bitter. It’s not that I’m trying to be picky, but when you’re working all day, you need something that actually tastes good. I completely agree. I think we’re all just looking for a little bit of comfort in our day, and a decent coffee is one of those things. It’s like a small treat for the soul. Exactly. I think we could all use a little bit more of that.

So, do you ever find it weird that social media is now like the main way people connect, even in libraries? I mean, I know we're all supposed to be about knowledge and information, but sometimes I feel like we're just posting about our coffee or our book recommendations instead of actually helping people. Yeah, I can't deny it. I mean, I use it for professional development, of course. But I also have this group chat with other librarians where we just spam each other with memes and random facts about books. It's kind of a weird mix of serious and silly. Oh, I totally get that. I mean, I used to work in a public library in New Zealand, and we had the same thing. One of our librarians started a Facebook group called “Librarians who are also into K-dramas.” It turned into this huge community of people who just wanted to talk about breakfasts and their weekend plans, but everyone still ended up helping each other with research. Haha, that’s a good one. I actually have a friend who’s a librarian and she’s on Twitter like, all the time. She puts out these tweets with obscure facts and then gets into arguments with people about whether something is true or not. It’s like a digital version of the old library debates. Yeah, I’ve seen that too. I once saw her argue about whether the moon was made of cheese. And she had like ten followers who were actually convinced it was. Who even knows what they were thinking. It’s amazing how people can get so passionate about things that are completely trivial. I guess it’s just part of the human condition, though. We all have to find ways to engage with the world, even if it’s through a screen. Exactly. And it’s not all bad. I mean, social media has made it so much easier for us to share resources, collaborate on projects, and even reach out to people in other countries. It’s just a bit of a double-edged sword. True. I think we just have to remember that we’re still here to help people find information, even if we’re also trying to keep up with the latest trends. Agreed. I mean, I still get asked by students if I can help them find a book, even if they’re just looking for a good read to binge on.

So, do you think we've got enough information to move forward with the business case for the new hospice? I mean, the location is still a bit of a sticking point, isn't it? I think we need to do a bit more consultation with the local health services. We’ve talked about it, but we haven't actually sat down with the NHS and the local GPs to get their input. They might have some valuable insights on where the demand is, and where we’d be most effective. That’s a good point. I’ve been in touch with the local Clinical Commissioning Group, and they seem interested. But we still need to formalise the consultation process. I was thinking we could organise a meeting with them next week, maybe on Thursday. That sounds doable. And what about the organisation of the local health services? We need to make sure that the new hospice can integrate smoothly with the existing care system. There’s a lot to consider in terms of referral pathways and coordination with other providers. Absolutely. One of the key rationales for the location is that it’s within a reasonable distance of several key health facilities. But we’ve still got to make sure that the proposed site is accessible and doesn’t cause any extra strain on the services. Also, we need to think about the relationship with the existing hospices in the area. We don’t want to be seen as competing with them, but rather complementing their services. It’s all about collaboration. Definitely. And regarding patient health and the nursing of people at the end of life, the new hospice should be designed with that in mind. The facilities need to be comfortable, supportive, and conducive to both physical and emotional well-being. We’ve had some preliminary ideas on the building design, but we might need to bring in some architects or consultants to make sure we’re on the right track. There’s a lot to consider in terms of layout, accessibility, and the overall patient experience. I agree. I was also thinking about the use of estate agents. We need to get professional help to find the right site. We can't just pick a location based on convenience alone—it has to be a strategic decision. That makes sense. And of course, we can’t forget about the politics and geography of the area.

I can't believe we've got to this point. I remember when we first met, it was like,  what are we doing here?  I know, I remember that too. You were so nervous about the job interview, weren't you? Yeah, I was. I mean, I had the qualifications, but I just felt like I wasn’t  right  for the role. That’s so common, isn’t it? You go through all that training, you get the interview, and then you just freeze. I think it’s the pressure. Especially when you’re in a new place, like the city, and you’ve got to impress people who don’t know you. It’s ridiculous, really. I mean, I had a friend who said, “Just be yourself—no one’s going to care!” But I didn’t listen. That’s the thing, though. You’re not just being yourself, you’re being  perfect . And that’s not real. Exactly. You know, I think that’s one of the reasons I’ve always preferred working in a team. You can offload some of that pressure. Speaking of pressure—I’ve been thinking about that Royal Ascot thing. You still going? Yeah, I’m going with my sister. She’s been talking about it for ages. I’m not sure why I’m going, though. It’s so posh. That’s the thing. Some people just love that sort of thing. I mean, I’ve got a cousin who insists on wearing a waistcoat and about five rings to every event. Oh, I had a friend like that once. She wore her engagement ring to a gas station. The guy behind the counter asked her if she was planning on getting married. Oh no. That’s not a good story. No, it’s not. But it’s true. We had to tell her she looked like a  political rally  trying to find a  shopping mall . Okay, that’s  not  a nice image. I know. I think it was more about her trying to be  unapologetically herself . You know, the kind of vibe that makes people uncomfortable. Yeah, and I think that’s the thing about being in your 30s. You start to understand that life isn’t about fitting in—it’s about making your own rules. I suppose. Although, honestly, I still feel like I’m trying too hard sometimes. You’re not.

I don’t think I can watch that horror film with you, I’ve had enough of jumping out of my skin already. Oh come on, it’s just a few jump scares. You’re being dramatic. No, it’s not just a few jump scares. It’s like every five minutes there’s a ghost or something. Yeah, but that’s the point. It’s supposed to be scary. Oh, I know it’s supposed to be scary, but I was already halfway through a cup of tea, and now I’ve spilt it on myself because of some random noise. You’re overreacting. It’s just a film. It’s not just a film. I felt like someone was in the room with me. I swear, the lights flickered and I heard a door creak. You’re just being paranoid. You know how I feel about these things. Yeah, I know, but I still think it’s creepy. I mean, the soundtrack is so loud and it just doesn’t stop. I think it’s more about the fact that we’re both watching it at night and it’s dark. That’s not helping, I’m not even sure if the room is dark. I’m just sitting here with my eyes wide open, trying not to look at the screen. Okay, maybe I should just stop the film. I don’t want you to have a panic attack. No, no, don’t stop it. I want to finish it. I just need a bit of a break. Alright, but if you start hyperventilating, I’m not helping you. You wouldn’t be able to. You’d be scared too. Maybe, but I’m not as sensitive as you. Oh, I’m not sensitive, I’m just… cautious. Yeah, but that’s what makes you the perfect horror film watcher. Yeah, maybe. But I still think I need a snack. Maybe some chocolate to go with it. Okay, but only if you promise not to scream when the final jump scare happens. Deal. But if I scream, it’s because I’m scared, not because I’m being dramatic. Alright, let’s just watch it and see if we can survive. I hope we do. I don’t think I’ve ever been this scared of a movie before. Oh, you’re going to be fine. You’re just getting used to it.

I just got a new iPad, so I thought I’d try to set it up properly before bed. Oh, nice! You’ve gone all digital then? Yeah, I thought it would be easier than carrying around my old phone and tablet. Well, I suppose it’s better than having to remember all your passwords on paper. Exactly! I used to keep them in a drawer, and I’d forget half of them. I still do that, actually. I keep my keys in a little tin with a note saying "Daniel’s keys" on it. That’s not very clever, though. You should use an app like Passcode or something. I tried, but I always forget the password, and then I have to call someone. Yeah, it’s so frustrating. I even tried using a password manager, but I couldn’t remember the master password. Oh, I know the feeling. I had to give up after a week. My brain’s just not up to it anymore. I’ve heard that’s common for people my age. It’s like our memory’s getting worse as we get older. I suppose it is. I’ve read that memory starts to decline in your 30s. Maybe that’s why I’ve started using more gadgets. It’s easier to just have everything in one place. I can see that. I’ve got a few smart speakers at home, and I use them to remind me of things. That’s a good idea. I’ve been trying to remember to buy the groceries, but I keep forgetting. You should set up some reminders on your phone. I do that for the postman and for the laundry. I did try that, but I kept turning it off because it was too annoying. I understand. I have a voice reminder that goes off every hour to say, “Daniel, take your pills.” It’s annoying, but it works. I might try that. I think the key is to go with what works for you, even if it’s a bit strange. Exactly. It’s all about finding the right balance. I guess that’s the thing with gadgets – they can help, but you can’t rely on them completely. True. You still need to be responsible for your own routine. I agree. I think I’ll just stick with my iPad for now and see how it goes.

So, do you remember that time we were in Morocco and we ended up staying in this little riad in Fez? It was supposed to be a quiet place, but we ended up getting chased out by a group of men who were arguing about whether or not the owner was a terrorist. Oh yeah, that was wild. I still remember the look on your face when you suddenly had to sprint down the narrow alleyway with a bag of mint tea in your hand. You looked like you were running from a stampede of camels. It was ridiculous. But it was also one of those moments that made the trip even more memorable. You can't plan for things like that, you know? Sometimes the best stories come from the chaos. Definitely. And you know what I love about travel? It gives you a chance to read books in places you wouldn’t normally get to. Like that time we were in Kyoto and I read this book about Japanese culture in a tiny café with tatami mats and a view of the gardens outside. It was perfect. Yeah, I remember that. I was reading  The Art of Seeing  by John Berger, and it really made me think about how context changes the way we experience something. Like how a book is different when you’re in a foreign place – it’s like you’re seeing it through new eyes. Exactly. And it’s not just books. It’s about how travel changes the way you think. Like, when I was in Edinburgh a few years ago, I picked up a copy of  The History of Scotland  and read it in the castle gardens. It felt like the past was literally under my feet. That’s a good way to put it. I think travel and reading both have this way of making you feel like you’re not just consuming knowledge – you’re living it. You’re part of the story. And that’s why I always say that the best books are the ones you read on the road. You don’t just read them, you live them. You carry them with you. It’s like the pages are full of footprints. I think that’s true. I’ve got a book I’m reading now called  The Road to Nowhere  by some guy from Glasgow. It’s about the journey of a man who leaves his country to find himself.

Mm, I just wanted to talk to you about the job application. I know it's been a bit of a process, and I’m feeling a bit overwhelmed. Of course, sweetheart, I’m here for you. What’s worrying you? Well, the application was due yesterday, and I didn't send it. I was so nervous about what they might think if I didn’t meet all the criteria. I mean, I have this postgraduate degree, but I’m not sure if that's enough. What if they’re looking for more experience? Honey, you have to remember that you're not just applying for a job. You're applying to work in a field where you have a lot of knowledge and passion. Your degree is solid, and your experience in architecture, even if it's not traditional, is still valuable. You’ve worked on some incredible projects, and that’s something they’ll notice. I know, but I keep second-guessing myself. I mean, I’ve always been the kind of person who wants to do everything perfectly, and I feel like I haven’t met the standard. You're not wrong to want to do things well, but perfection isn’t the goal here—it’s about showing your strengths and being honest about your abilities. You’ve got talent, and I’ve seen it. Don’t let self-doubt hold you back. You always say that, and it helps, but it's hard. I also feel like I'm not as experienced as some of the other candidates. What if I don’t get the job? That’s exactly why it’s important to apply. You don’t know what you’re missing out on if you don’t try. And even if you don’t get it, it’s still an opportunity to learn and grow. You’re not just applying for a job; you’re applying for a chance to show who you are. You’re right. I just wish I could be more confident. I’m trying so hard to be, but it’s not always easy. I know it’s not easy, but you're not alone in this. I’ve been there too. Remember, you’re not just applying for a job—you're applying to work in a field you care about, and that’s something to be proud of. If you don’t send it now, you’ll always wonder what could have been.

Well, it’s a lovely day today, isn't it? Not too hot, just the right kind of spring weather. You know, I always say that the best time of year is when the ground is still a little bit damp from the rain and the sun comes out to dry it off. I agree with you, old chap. It’s the kind of day that makes you think about the old days—when we used to have proper gardens and a shed full of tools. Now, you can’t even get a decent shed these days without having to go through a whole council application process. Oh, I know. I used to have a lovely little garden when I was still running the nursery. But now, you’ve got to get planning permission just to put a bird feeder up, let alone build a shed. It’s all so complicated. It is, isn’t it? And when you think about it, this country’s got more rules in place than a shop selling takeaway food. You can’t even park your car in the street without getting a ticket, let alone get it out of the driveway without a permit. Aye, and don’t get me started on the cars. These days, you can't just trot out a little old Ford Fiesta and call it a day. You’ve got to have a car that’s got all these safety features and emissions standards. I remember when we all used to drive around in ‘60s cars with no airbags and just a bit of tin for a body. That’s true. I remember when my father used to have a red Ford Anglia. It was a bit crude, but it ran fine and it was about as safe as a sack of feathers. Now, the cars are so complicated, they even have to have failsafe systems that stop you from starting the engine if you're not wearing a seatbelt. Yes, well, I suppose it's for the best. Safety first. But I do sometimes think that the government’s more interested in restricting people’s freedom than actually solving the problems. Take housing, for example. You've got more people needing a home than ever before, yet the supply is dwindling and the prices are going through the roof. Mm, that's a real shame. I remember when we were young, we could afford a house with a bit of savings and a bit of luck.

So, do you think we've got enough space to convert that little corner into a new office for the marketing team? It's been a bit of a bottleneck lately with everyone trying to fit in their workstations. I think we could. The acoustics in that area are decent, and we’ve got the fire escape access right there. It would be good to have a dedicated space for them to focus on campaigns without constantly bumping into each other. Yeah, but we need to make sure we don’t disrupt the existing tenants. They’ve been pretty sensitive about noise and the layout. I remember last week, one of them mentioned that the new storage cupboard we added was a bit of a pain to access. Touché. I should talk to the tenant liaison team about it. They’re the ones who can handle any concerns. Also, have you seen the latest bookings? The upcoming weekends are almost full, so we might need to look into hiring a temporary staff member to cover the extra hours. I saw that. We’re going to have to start advertising again for part-time help, maybe even some holiday cover. It’s getting a bit tight. I agree. We’ve got a few vacancies on the roster, and we’re not getting enough applications. Maybe we can partner with a local university or college, like the one just across the street. They often have students looking for part-time work. That could work. We could even offer them some training on our systems. It’s also a good way to build a relationship with the local community. Speaking of community, the marketing team mentioned a new campaign for the weekend music events – they want to promote it better, maybe with some social media content. Interesting. I think we could use some help with that too. Maybe someone from the design team could assist with creating visuals. We should also consider the furniture. The old desks and chairs are starting to look a bit tired. The new furniture we’re thinking of buying has some eco-friendly options. I’ve been looking into some sustainable furniture options too. It could be a good selling point for our tenants who are into green living. Plus, it’s better for the environment. Exactly. We should make sure the new goings-on in the building are communicated clearly to everyone.

I can’t believe how good this roast is. It’s like it’s been slow cooked for days, but it’s actually only been in the oven for an hour. Yeah, I mean, it’s Chef’s fault. He said it’s a “Wales-to-England” slow roast—whatever that means. Oh, I know what he means. It’s like a Welsh roast but with a British twist. I think he’s trying to be the best of both worlds. It’s working, though. The sauce is perfect, and the potatoes are just right—crispy on the outside, soft on the inside. Yeah, I’ve had that same sauce on my mind all week. I think I dreamt about it last night. You and me both. I had a dream about a roast so good it made me cry. I woke up with a full stomach and a wet pillow. That’s not surprising, though. You’ve been eating too much of that comfort food from the shop. Well, it’s not just comfort food. It’s  delicious  food. And Chef’s got a real talent for it. He’s got a good ear for what people like. He’s got this knack for making everything taste like it’s from a proper restaurant. I still can’t believe he’s a chef and not a food critic. He’s got the same taste as the Michelin-starred ones. He’s got a point. I mean, the way he comes up with these recipes—it’s like he’s got a secret menu about how to make every day feel like a celebration. I think it’s all about the spices. He uses the right ones, and it just makes everything better. And the way he talks about food. He’s got this way of making even the simplest meal feel special. I think it’s because he’s been in the kitchen so long. I mean, he’s been cooking since he was a kid. Yeah, he’s got a proper background. He used to work in the city, but he said he missed the countryside, so he moved back here. And now he’s got this little cottage, and he’s cooking for all of us. It’s like a dream come true. And we’re all just lucky enough to be here, eating like royalty. I think this is the best meal I’ve had in ages.

So, do you think we should go to Manchester for the weekend? I’ve been meaning to visit the new brewery there, and I heard they have a really cool music scene. Manchester? You mean the one with the underground? I mean, it’s a bit far from here, but if it’s for the music, I’d say yes. But have you got any specific plans? Not yet, but I was thinking of hitting up a few venues. I heard there’s a new place called The Castle that’s supposed to be amazing. Plus, I want to check out the city centre again. It’s been a while. That sounds good, but have you thought about the cost? I mean, Manchester isn’t exactly cheap. The transport, the food, the accommodation... You know, I’d say we should plan the budget first. Yeah, I guess. But I was thinking we could just camp in a car park or something. I heard the city has some pretty cool spots for that. Also, the pubs there are usually more affordable. Oh, I’ve heard about that. But don’t you think it might be a bit risky? I mean, there are rules about that now. Plus, it’s not like we’re in the countryside. I know, but I think it’s still allowed. I mean, not everywhere, but some places. If we go to the Castle, maybe we can just park in the area and walk. Yeah, but have you thought about the weather? It’s still winter, and it can get pretty cold. Even in Manchester. You might need a jacket or something. Right, but I’m not going to be outside all the time. I’ll just go in and out. Plus, I’ve got a few friends who live there, so I could stay with them. That’d save us money on accommodation. That’s a good point. I mean, if you can meet up with your friends, that could be cheaper than staying in a hotel. But do you know if they’ll be there? I think they’ll be there for the weekend. I’ve messaged them, and they said they’re free. They’ve even offered to cook for us. Oh, that’s great. Cooking with friends can be fun. But what about the food? I mean, Manchester has some good places, but I’m not sure about the local cuisine.

So, do you know how it's going with your mum? I heard she had her operation last week. Yeah, it went okay, I think. She’s been feeling a bit shaky since then, but the doctors said it was a success. That’s good to hear. I’m sorry to hear about the operation, though. I know how scary that can be. It was. She’s been through a lot lately. Not just the operation, but there’s been a lot of stress in the family. I can only imagine. It’s tough when someone you love is going through something like that. How are the rest of the family dealing with it? Honestly, it’s been a bit of a mess. My dad’s been really upset, and my brother’s been avoiding talking about it. It’s like he doesn’t want to face it. That’s sad. I think it’s normal to feel that way, especially with something as heavy as losing a parent. It’s hard to process. Yeah, I know. And I don’t think anyone’s really talked about what’s going to happen next. The funeral, the arrangements… it’s all so overwhelming. I can’t imagine. I’m sorry, but I know how important it is to plan things out. It’s not just about the funeral, it’s about making sure everything’s taken care of. It is. But I don’t know where to start. I’ve been trying to email the family, but some people aren’t responding. That’s so frustrating. Maybe you should try talking to someone about it? Like a funeral director or a councillor? They can help with the planning and also with the emotional stuff. I’m not sure. I don’t want to burden anyone else. You don’t have to. It’s okay to ask for help. You’re not alone in this. Everyone grieves differently, and it’s important to take time for yourself. I guess. It’s just hard to admit that I need support. I’m still trying to wrap my head around the whole thing. That’s totally normal. I think one of the hardest parts is just accepting that your mum isn’t coming back. Yeah, I know. It’s like, every day I think, ‘What would she say if she saw me now?’ And I don’t even know how to answer that.

So, do you know what’s on your agenda for the holidays, boys? Not really... I was thinking of just staying local, maybe going to a football match or something. Yeah, me too. I’ve got a few mates who are going to the Lake District. I think we’re going to rent a cabin for the weekend. Sounds nice. I’ve been thinking about a bit of skiing in the Alps. Skiing? You’re gonna do that again? You’ve done it every year since you were 15. It’s not just about the skiing. It’s the whole experience, the culture, the food. You know, the wine. Oh, you’re into wine, are you? I’ve been learning about it. It’s actually a big part of what I do at work—proofing wine labels and stuff. I’ve got a few clients who are into high-end stuff, so I’ve had to get pretty clued up on the different regions and vintages. Yeah, I know what you mean. We had a few clients in Korea who were really into wine. I used to take them to a little winery near Seoul. Wait, you’re from Seoul? Yeah, I was born there, but I’ve been in the UK for over twenty years now. That’s cool. I’ve never been to Asia. I can definitely tell you about the food and the culture. You know, it’s not just about the big cities. There’s a lot of small villages with really authentic places. That’s interesting. I’ve always thought of Korea as being very modern, but I guess there’s more to it. Yeah, I mean, I’ve seen some videos of food markets there. They look amazing. I’d love to go one day. You should. I could take you. That’d be awesome. And speaking of holidays, have you thought about work experience for the summer? Not really. I go to a secondary school, so I guess I’m not exactly in a position to apply for work experience. Me neither. I’m just waiting for the school to send out the forms. Well, if you’re interested, I know a few companies in the area that might be looking for students. I can put you in touch. Yeah, I know a few places too. Maybe we can all get together and apply for something.

So, do you remember that trip we took to Japan a few years back? I still have those old photos on my phone, and I was just flicking through them the other day. Oh yes, I remember that! I still have the little notebook you bought me with all those funny phrases in it. I tried to use it in Tokyo, but I mostly ended up just pointing and laughing. That’s the spirit! I think I got a few decent shots too. There was that one of the cherry blossoms in Kyoto—do you remember that? It was so peaceful. Yes! I think that’s the one with the little shrine in the background. You were trying to take a photo of the petals falling, but the wind was so strong, you ended up with a blur of pink and white. I think it turned out pretty cool, though. Ha! I remember that. I was so proud of myself for getting the exposure right, even though the subject was, you know, kind of chaotic. It’s funny how those photos feel like they’re from another life. I mean, we were both so young and full of energy back then. Do you think we’d be able to go back? I’d love to. I’ve been thinking about it a lot. There’s something about Japan that just feels… timeless. Even now, when I look at the photos, I can almost hear the sounds and smell the air. I know. And I still have that badger photo we took in the countryside—do you remember? You were so obsessed with it. Oh, that badger! I still get a laugh every time I see it. You remember how we followed it for what felt like hours? I remember! You were convinced it was going to lead us to a hidden treasure. I was! I even bought a compass and everything. And you know what? It actually led us to a lovely little stream. So it wasn’t all in vain. Even if it didn’t have gold or anything. Exactly. And besides, the photo’s a keeper. Maybe one day we go back to the same spot and see if that badger’s still around. I’d like that. It would be a nice little adventure. I’ll start planning. You can be the wildlife expert and I’ll handle the photos.

So, do you remember that time we were in Ireland and we ended up getting lost in the middle of nowhere? Oh yeah, I still remember that. We were on our way to a pub and suddenly we were surrounded by sheep and the GPS said we were in a village called "Boring". I think that’s the one. I was so hungry I wanted to just eat a sheep. That’s not a real place, though. I mean, it’s not like you can actually find it on a map. Yeah, but the moment we got to the pub, we realized we were in a pretty cool spot. They had these massive portions of fish and chips. Oh, you’re telling me. I was so full I couldn’t even dance properly. I think I just sat down and fell asleep for an hour. That sounds like you. You were always the one who ate the most, even when we were in Australia, ordering double portions of meat pies. I mean, it’s not like we were in a place where food was scarce. In fact, in Sydney, I think the only thing more plentiful than food was the amount of people who snored when they got home. Speaking of snoring, I swear one time in London, my flatmate snored so loud that it woke up the entire building. I went to the council and they said they couldn’t do anything because it was “a natural occurrence.” That’s not natural. That’s just rude. I once had a roommate who snored so loudly that I had to sleep with earplugs and a fan. I know the feeling. My brother used to snore like a chainsaw. One night I woke up and thought it was a robber breaking in. You know, if that’s the case, maybe we should all start recording our snoring. I heard there’s an app called “SnoreTracker” or something like that. Yeah, but I think it’s called “Sleepy Snore” or “Snore Detection.” Anyway, I think it’s something you can download on your phone. I tried it once. It said I was at a “high snoring risk.” I was like, “Thanks, I already know that.” Maybe it’s better to just live with it. I mean, if you think about it, snoring is kind of like a sound effect in a horror movie.

So, do you ever just sit down and play computer games for ages? I mean, it’s like,  what  do you do with them? I know, right? I think I’ve been doing that more lately. I’ve been trying to get through this new game that’s come out—something like  The Witcher 4  or whatever. But honestly, I’m just… not very good at it. I keep dying. I can imagine. I used to play a lot of games when I was younger, like  Grand Theft Auto  or  Call of Duty . But now I just… I don’t know. I’ve got a baby and a PhD, and I’ve got  zero  time to play. I’ve even got to think about things like border security, which is like,  why  would anyone want to play a game about that? Oh, I’ve thought about that too. I mean, it’s a bit weird, isn’t it? Like, how do they even make a game about border security? I mean, I’ve seen some really odd things, like games where you’re a spy or something. But border security? It feels like it’s more of a topic for a documentary or a news report. Yeah, I mean, maybe the games are just trying to be edgy, but they don’t really do the subject justice. It’s not like you can just  simulate  the real-world challenges of immigration or security checks. Like, someone could be in a game, and you can just walk through the gate, but in real life, you’d have to go through a whole process. Exactly! It’s like they make it too easy. I mean, I’ve had to wait in queues at airports for hours. And I’ve seen people get refused entry for all sorts of reasons. It’s not just about being there. It’s about proving you’re not a threat. And that’s not something that games really capture. I know, it’s a bit of a shame. You’d think with all the technology we have, we could make games that are more realistic. But then again, maybe that’s the point—games are supposed to be fun, not a simulation. Yeah, I guess. I mean, if you’re going to play a game about border security, you’d probably want it to be more like  The Sims  than some kind of war game.

So, do you know, I’ve been thinking about going rowing again. It’s been a while since I last got on the water, and I’ve been feeling pretty motivated lately. I've been reading about it and it seems like it could be a great way to get back in shape. That sounds nice. I’ve always wanted to try rowing too. I think it’s one of those things you’ve got to experience to really know if you like it. I remember when I was younger, my dad used to take me kayaking on the lake near Shipley when I was a kid. It was a lot of fun, even if I did end up falling in once and had to climb out of the water like a drowned rat. Oh, I can imagine. I’ve had my share of mishaps too, especially when I was learning to paddle. But I think it’s all part of the process, isn’t it? You just have to keep trying. Exactly. Although, I have to admit, the first time I tried rowing, I felt completely out of my depth—literally and metaphorically. I mean, the rhythmic motion is so different from anything else, and I think it takes a while to get the timing right. I can see that. I’ve been trying to learn how to row at a local club, and honestly, it’s harder than I thought. You’ve got to coordinate your movements with your body, and the boat feels like it’s always trying to move in the opposite direction. It’s quite the challenge. I know what you mean. It’s not just about the physical effort; it’s also about the mental focus. I think that’s why I’m still interested in it. I remember when I first met my sister after she moved back to England from France. We hadn’t seen each other in years, and it was like we were strangers again. It was strange, but also incredibly emotional. Wow, that must have been intense. I can only imagine how that felt. I lost my mum last year, and it’s still so hard to talk about sometimes. It’s funny how things change, isn’t it? It really is. That’s one of the reasons I think it’s important to keep up with family, even if it’s just through regular calls or visits.

Dad, do you know how to type in Morse code? Not really, love. I know the basics, but I don’t use it much anymore. Why? I was just thinking… I saw some messages online where people use dots and dashes like in Morse code. It’s kind of cool, isn’t it? Yeah, it is. Back in the day, we used it to communicate over long distances. I used to listen to Morse code on the radio as a kid. It was the only way to get messages during the war or stuff. Wow, that’s so old-school. I mean, we’ve got text messages, emojis, and everything now. Yeah, and it’s all much quicker. But I still think Morse code is pretty clever. I mean, you can send messages with just dots and dashes. Maybe I should try learning it. It could be useful if my phone’s out of battery or something. That could be a good skill to have. But I wouldn’t recommend trying it on your phone—unless you want to get your friends confused. Haha, maybe. But I was also wondering, why do people use so many emojis these days? Like, they’re just pictures, right? Yeah, but they’re a shorthand for emotions. Sometimes you can’t really capture the tone of a message with just words. Emojis make it easier to understand how someone feels. I guess. But I still think it’s a bit weird. Like, sometimes people use too many. Oh, I know. I’ve seen messages with a whole bunch of emojis and no real words. It’s like a language of its own. I mean, it’s kind of fun to do. But I’m still trying to figure out how to spell my name in Morse code. Let me help you. First, I’ll write it out in letters, then we’ll convert it to dots and dashes. Okay, so M-A-R-Y? M is dot-dot, A is dot-dash, R is dash-dot-dot, Y is dash-dot-dash-dot. That’s a lot of dashes. Yeah, it can get confusing. But it’s a good way to practice. Wait, so if I had to send a message to my friend about going to the shops, how would that work? You’d need to convert each word into Morse code. It’s not as fast as texting, but it’s a cool skill.

Yo, man, it's been ages! You're looking good. How's life treating you? Yo, I'm good, man. It's been a while, but I've been keeping busy. How about you? Still stuck in the university grind? Yeah, I'm still there, but I'm getting more into it than ever. I reckon I'm going to do a master’s in something tech-related. Maybe AI or something like that. You ever think about that? Honestly, I've been thinking about it too. But honestly, I don't know if I'm ready for that level of work. I mean, I love learning, but I'm still trying to figure out what I'm going to do after this. You ever think about working in Japan? I heard Tokyo is awesome, and they're always looking for people with tech skills. Yeah, I've been thinking about Japan a lot lately. I mean, I know it's a bit far, but I've been watching some anime and eating some of that ramen I saw on YouTube—so I'm like, maybe one day I can go over there. You ever think about that? For real? I did go on a trip to Japan last year, actually. It was insane. The food, the culture, everything. I almost stayed longer, but my sister wanted me back. But seriously, if you ever go, you've got to try the ramen at that little place in Shibuya. It's legit one of the best things I've ever had. Oh man, you had to be there. I've been looking up ramen places in London, but it's not the same. I mean, I know it's not the same as the real thing, but I'm starting to think about maybe taking a trip to Japan after I finish my degree. You ever think about doing something like that? Definitely. I mean, I can't just stay in London forever. It's too expensive, and I’ve been hearing about how people in Tokyo are making a lot of money in tech. Maybe I can work there once I finish my degree. It's a long shot, but I'm not ruling it out. That’s the spirit. I go to a few tech cafes here sometimes, and it’s wild how much people are talking about Japan and how they’re building up their tech scene.

So, do you remember that time we went to Buckfast Abbey? I still can’t get over how peaceful it was, and the monks were so friendly. It was like stepping back in time. Oh, yes, I remember that. That place is like a little sanctuary. And that monk who gave us the tea—oh, he had this twitch in his eye, like he was trying not to laugh. I’ve never seen anyone so serious and so funny at the same time. I remember that too. We had to climb up the hill, and I was so out of breath. I thought I was going to collapse. I mean, I’m 90 and I’ve only done that once in my life. You did it though, and you didn’t even need a walking stick. I still feel guilty for laughing when you turned around and had that look on your face like you’d been defeated by a hill. Oh, I wasn’t defeated. I was exploring the spiritual side of life. You have to embrace the journey, not just the destination. I get that, but I still think I’d be better off taking a cruise. You know, just to get out of the country and not have to deal with all this British weather. I mean, it’s been raining every day this week, and I’ve had enough of wet shoes. I did a cruise once, actually. It was in the Caribbean. I had a good time, although someone kept asking me for money. I think they thought I was a retired accountant with a lot of cash. I told them I was just a humble pensioner. That’s a good story. I’ve heard that people think retired accountants are the most moneyed people in the world. I suppose it’s because of the way we talk—slow and deliberate, like we’re always calculating something. Maybe that’s why we should all learn to use technology better. Like, the phone. I was trying to set up a reminder yesterday, and I couldn’t figure out how. It was like learning how to use a calculator again. I think it’s all about patience, love, and a little bit of common sense. Plus, if you don’t know, you can always ask someone. Like me. You’re the one who got confused between a Facebook post and a message on your phone.

Mum, Dad, I've got so much to tell you! How was Belgium? Did you enjoy it? Oh, it was lovely, really. We had a great time. The weather was good, and we got to see some beautiful countryside. We even cycled a bit. Yes, and the food was absolutely amazing. We had this little market in Brussels where they sold all these fresh cheeses and chocolate. I bought some truffles too, but honestly, I don't know what I did with them. They were so expensive! Oh no, I hope you didn’t waste them! You know how much they cost. I mean, truffles are like, you can’t just throw them away. I know, I know. It was just a bit of a shock when I got them. I thought, “Oh, this is going to be a treat,” but then I looked at the price tag and just…  shuddered . And then there was the sat nav. I thought it was going to be helpful, but it was a total nightmare. It told us to take this really long, winding road through the countryside, and we ended up getting lost for like 45 minutes. We had to ask a local for directions. Oh no, that’s the worst! I remember that time in France when we had to rely on a map and a compass. It’s like the sat nav is just a fancy way of making you more confused. Honestly, I think it was a bit of a test. I mean, you don’t just go abroad without a bit of a challenge, right? Oh, and then there was the driving. I couldn’t believe how different it was. We were used to driving on the left, but in Belgium, it’s the right. It took a while to get used to. I nearly got into an accident once when I was trying to park. That’s scary! I was driving in Italy once and I tried to reverse into a space, but I ended up crashing into a wall. I’ve never been so embarrassed in my life. That sounds just like you. You always do things the hard way. Yeah, go on, tell us more about your trip. What was the best part? Oh, the markets were the best. There’s this one in Ghent that’s just so lively. We got to try all these local foods—like waffles and mussels.

I just thought I'd try making this new recipe I found online. It's a herby chicken dish with a side of roasted vegetables. I thought it would be nice for dinner tonight. Sounds good. I’ve been craving something a bit different from our usual roast dinner. Maybe it’s time we stepped out of our comfort zone. I agree. I wanted to try something with a bit more flavor. I added some thyme and rosemary to the chicken, and the vegetables are roasted with olive oil and garlic. That sounds lovely. I might even try adding some lemon zest to the chicken. I’ve been meaning to experiment with more citrus in my cooking. My mother always said that cooking is like perfume — it’s about the layers, the balance, and the way it makes people feel. Do you think that’s true? Absolutely. I think it’s more than just taste. It’s about the aroma, the way the food looks, and how it makes people feel when they eat it. I remember when I first moved to London, the way the food smelled in the market reminded me of home. I love that. It reminds me of my childhood, when my grandmother used to cook with all these beautiful herbs. She always said it was about the love you put into it. That’s the thing about cooking — it can be a way to connect with people, even if you’re just sharing a meal. I think that’s also why I’ve been thinking a lot about our friends on Facebook lately. Yes, I know. It’s funny how social media can bring people together, even if we don’t see them every day. I’ve been trying to catch up with some of them, but it’s not the same as actually meeting up. Definitely not. I think there’s something special about being in the same room, sharing a meal, and just talking. Speaking of which, have you ever thought about having a fireplace in our living room? I’ve been dreaming about it for ages. A fireplace? I think it would be perfect for the winter. It would add that cozy, warm feeling to the house. I’ve been thinking about buying some really nice wood and some scented candles to go with it. I’d love that. Maybe we can even get some flowers to go with it — something that can be moved around and changed with the seasons.

I've just heard from an old colleague of mine who used to teach in Brisbane. He's been there for years, and he says it's absolutely freezing now. Oh, I thought it was hotter than hell. I mean, I went to Queensland once on a holiday. It was so hot, I couldn’t even eat properly. Yeah, but I read somewhere that they have a different kind of climate there. Not the same as the Australian outback, but still, it's not like England. That's true. I mean, I've never been to Australia, but I've heard so many stories. I think some people from the north of England go there for the summer and then come back in the winter with a tan. I think I know someone who worked there for a while. He said he had to wear suits all the time, even in the heat, because of the way the business men dress down there. It’s like they’re all trying to look like they’re from London. I can imagine. I mean, even in Sheffield, we have our own kind of way of dressing. You can tell if someone’s from the north by the way they wear their coats. Oh, yes. I remember when I was teaching in Bristol, I used to get so many students who said they were from the south. But when they spoke, you could tell they weren’t from the South of England, they were from the North. And not just in terms of accent. I mean, the way they talk, the way they say things. It’s like they have their own dialect. I think it's called the Sheffield dialect. I know it's different from the way people from Manchester or Liverpool speak. It’s more of a drawl, if you like. Yeah, that's what I always thought. I used to work with people from Sheffield, and they would always say things like “I bin” instead of “I’ve been”. It was so different from the way people from Bristol or London spoke. I think it's partly because of the way the industrial areas developed. I mean, places like Sheffield and Manchester had a lot of steelworks and factories, so the working class grew up with a certain kind of language. Exactly. And then there’s the way people from the south speak.

So, do you ever find it hard to stay off social media? I mean, it's like it's everywhere, isn't it? I can't even go to the bathroom without checking my phone. Honestly, I think I do. I try to limit it, but sometimes when I'm in a place like this, with no signal, I just feel like I’m missing out on something. Like, I miss seeing what my friends are up to, even if I’m not posting much myself. I get that. It’s like the whole world is in your pocket now. But I’ve started to think that maybe it’s just better to take a break sometimes. Like, I’ve been trying to focus more on podcasts and actually listen to them instead of just scrolling through Instagram. It’s kind of like a digital detox, but I’m not sure if I’m doing it right. Oh, I’ve heard of that. I think it’s called a digital detox, right? I’ve tried it a few times, but honestly, it’s so hard. I just feel like I need to know what’s going on in the world, even if it’s just through a few quick scrolls. I mean, without social media, how would I even know what’s trending? That’s true. I guess it’s like a habit, isn’t it? You start off using it for real reasons, like staying in touch with friends or following what’s happening in the world, and then it just becomes this constant distraction. I think I’m trying to read more books instead of watching TV, but I’m not sure if that’s working. I mean, it’s hard to concentrate when I’m in a place like this, where everything is so quiet. Yeah, I feel you. I’ve been trying to watch more documentaries instead of binge-watching shows. It’s a bit more meaningful, I think, even if it’s not always as entertaining. I mean, I’ve been watching one about the history of podcasts. It was fascinating. I didn’t know how far back they went! Oh, that sounds interesting. I’ve always been curious about the origins of podcasts. I guess I never really thought about how they started. I mean, it’s such a big part of modern life now, but it’s amazing how something like that can evolve so quickly.

Alright, Pippy, you ready for your Blue Peter badge? I think we need to get your photo done first. I think I’ve got my passport already, Mummy. I showed it to the postman yesterday. I saw the postman, too. He was in a hurry, and he said he’s been working late all week. I think he's been trying to get a holiday. That's nice of him. But I don’t think you need a passport for the Blue Peter badge. Wait, are you sure you're allowed to get the badge at your age? I think it's for kids who are 10, and I’m 10. My friend Lucy got hers last week. She said it's really cool. You get a badge and a certificate, and then you can be a Blue Peter badge holder for a year! That does sound great. But I think you need a photo in a specific style, you know, like the one on the back of the envelope. Are you excited about it? Can I get one too? I want to be a Blue Peter badge holder as well. I think I can do it. I’ve got a smile that would make any camera happy! Oh, you’re such a show-off, Blue. Let’s just get your photo done first, and then maybe we can talk about the circus. The Travelling Circus? I saw the posters at the market. It’s coming to Norwich next week. Are we going? That’s a good question. It depends on the weather and whether we can get all the permissions from the council. Also, I need to check if we have enough pocket money for the tickets. I’ve got some pocket money. I got it from my grandma for helping her water the plants. She said I was a little gardener! That’s very kind of her. I think it’s a great idea. We can get the tickets and then maybe go to the circus together. But first, we need to get your photo done, Pippy. You need to look your best. I know! I’ve been practicing my smile every day. I even asked my dad to take a photo of me. He said I looked like a very happy little pirate. I saw a pirate on the TV once. He had a big red hat and a sword.

I just got a message from my cousin, and she’s been going on about this guy she met who has erectile dysfunction. She’s like, “It’s so frustrating, I can’t even tell if he’s interested.” Oh no, that’s not ideal.
