I remember once I saw him outside at lunchtime with a bag full of bits and pieces, like little miniature train tracks and things. I thought he was going to build a whole railway system in the playground. Yeah, and then there was Mrs. Green. I think she had a secret passion for detective stories. She’d always be reading those thick books in the staff room, and she’d give us riddles during break time. That was the best part. You’d never know she was into that stuff. I once overheard her talking to the head about a mystery novel she was writing. She even got it published, if I remember rightly. That’s right. Her book was about a teacher who disappears in the woods. It was so good – even the principal got a copy, and he said it was his favorite book of all time. It was a bit strange, though. Strange? She made it up? Like, someone actually disappearing in the woods? It was fictional, obviously. But what made it weird is that she used the real names of people in the school. I think she even used my name in one of the chapters. Oh no! She must have been really close to you. I mean, that was a while back, wasn’t it? Maybe she just thought she was being creative. I don’t know. I think it was a bit of a joke. But I can’t help but wonder if she knew something about the school that we didn't. Or maybe it was just a hobby. I mean, people do have all sorts of secrets. Still, I think it’s interesting how some of the things we go through in school stay with you. True. I remember once, when I was about 12, I tried to cheat at a geography quiz. I asked the teacher if I could use a map during the test.

Mum, do you remember when we were kids and we used to go to the market on Saturday mornings? I think I got a free sample of some weird fish once. Oh, I remember that! You were always trying to get your hands on the weirdest things. What was it called again? The weaver fish? Yeah, that’s what I think it was. It looked like a cross between a flake and a piece of seaweed. I tried to eat it, and it was like chewing a rubber band. You laughed at me for ages. I did! You were so determined to be adventurous, even when it was just a bait fish. Still, you’ve grown up to be an English teacher. I guess you’ve found your own kind of adventure. You could say that. I’ve been teaching for almost three years now, and it’s been amazing. I get to travel a lot too, which helps with the jet lag I’ve been getting. I just came back from Barcelona last week. Oh, Barcelona! I remember when you were a child and we used to listen to the radio about the city. You were always saying you wanted to live there. Have you ever thought about moving? Well, I’ve been thinking about it – especially with the new job I got in Manchester. It’s a bit of a commute, but the opportunities are better. Plus, I’ve been working with some amazing people. That sounds great. But are you sure you don’t want to stay here? You know, I’m thinking about getting a new place soon. I’ve been here for over twenty years, and it’s starting to feel a bit small. I need more space for the kids – or the cats, as you call them. Yeah, that makes sense. I mean, it’s not like we’re the only ones in the house. There’s always the dogs and the cats. But I have to say, it’s a bit of a hassle trying to keep up with them all. Ha! You know what I mean. But seriously, if you ever want to move, I’d be more than happy to help. You’ve always been the one with the better sense of direction than me. You know what? If I end up moving, I’ll definitely let you know. And maybe you could come stay with me for a while.

I can't believe the NHS is still struggling like this. It's been ages since I had to wait for anything, but now it's like everyone’s got a crisis. Yeah, I know. I was at the clinic last week for a minor infection and I waited for over two hours. It’s not just the wait, it’s the lack of resources. They’ve got so many people relying on them. I know, and I heard about the A-Level reforms. It’s all about making it more rigorous, but I don’t think it’s helping. The kids are under more pressure than ever, and it’s mostly just making them stressed. I agree. I think they’re trying to make it more like university, but not everyone is cut out for that kind of academic pressure. It’s a bit sad, honestly. Yeah, but I suppose it’s a way to keep up with the changing job market. I mean, if you want to get into a good university, you need good A-Levels. But I still don’t like the way it’s being forced on everyone. Fair point. I think it’s more about the competition, though. If you’re not on track, it’s easy to fall behind. I’ve seen friends who are really bright but just aren’t pushing themselves because they don’t see the point. It’s a real shame. I hope they reconsider some of the changes, but I also know that education is always evolving. Let’s not forget, though, that there’s also the petrol crisis. I was at the station this morning, and it’s like a stampede every time they announce a new price. Yeah, I saw the headlines. It’s crazy. I mean, what’s the point of having such a high standard of living if fuel prices keep going up? It just puts more pressure on people’s budgets. Exactly. I was thinking about the cost of living too. With all the changes in education, the NHS, and fuel, it’s really hard to keep up. I’m not sure how people with lower incomes are managing it all. I know. It’s a real worry. I think the government needs to go back to basics and figure out how to support everyone properly. But I guess we’ll just have to keep pushing through.

So, do you think we should still be smoking in the garden? I mean, it's not like we’re doing it in front of anyone, but I’m just not sure if it's the best idea anymore. Honestly, I don’t know. I mean, I like the idea of doing it on the balcony when we’re all together, but I’ve been thinking about the health stuff. You know, with everything that’s going on with the pandemic and all, maybe we should just cut it out. Yeah, but it's not like we’re outside all the time. And we’re not even like, smoking like crazy. It’s just a couple of cigarettes every now and then. But what if someone walks by? I mean, not that we’re doing anything wrong, but I don’t want to get caught. Especially not with all the health warnings now. Yeah, I get that. But I feel like everyone’s doing it in some way. I mean, not everyone, but some people. I think it’s just a habit, and it’s not like we’re hurting anyone. I guess that’s true. But I’ve read a few articles about how even light smoking can have long-term effects. Plus, I’m trying to stay away from all that stuff. I’m at university, and I want to stay healthy. I’m trying too. It’s just that it’s so hard when you’re with your mates, and you’re just like, "Why not?" But maybe we can just try to cut down. Yeah, maybe. I mean, I don’t smoke that much anyway. I think it’s more about the social aspect. Like, it’s a way to hang out and talk. But I get where you’re coming from. I know. I mean, it’s not like we’re doing anything wrong. But I do like the idea of being more responsible. Especially with all the money we’re spending on cigarettes. It’s not like we can afford to waste it. Exactly. And I think that’s part of what’s got me thinking about it too. Like, we’re all in university, and we’re trying to save money. Plus, we’ve got so much goin’ on with work, assignments, and everything else. I don’t want to waste money on something that could be a big problem later.

So, do you ever just… feel like you want to stop seeing someone? Like, not because they’re bad, but just because… you’re done? Yeah, I think I’ve been there. It’s weird, isn’t it? You know you’re still friends, but you don’t want to hang out anymore. It’s like… you just feel out of sync. Exactly. I had this with someone I used to be super close with. We used to talk every day, go out, do everything together. And then one day, it just… didn’t feel right anymore. I didn’t want to make the effort. I get that. It’s like you stop enjoying their company. You start thinking, “Why am I even doing this?” And then you realize, maybe it’s not about them—it’s about you. Yeah, it’s like when you’re in a relationship and you’re just… not feeling it anymore, but you’re too scared to say anything. You keep going through the motions, but it’s not fulfilling. Exactly. And sometimes, I think it’s not about being unkind. It’s more like… you’re just not on the same page anymore. You both have different priorities, different goals, and it’s hard to reconcile that. Totally. I mean, I’m not saying you have to be best friends forever, but there’s a point where you just… don’t want someone in your life anymore. And it’s tough because you don’t want to hurt their feelings, but you also don’t want to be fake. That’s the tricky part, isn’t it? You don’t want to be the one to end it, but you also don’t want to be the one stuck in that limbo. I mean, how do you even say it? Like, “Hey, I’ve been thinking about this, and I think we just aren’t clicking as much anymore.” Yeah, that’s exactly it. You have to be honest, but you have to be kind. It’s like trying to find the right balance between being authentic and being considerate. I think the best way is just to slowly back off. Like, start skipping plans here and there, or just not respond as much. Give them space to figure it out, too. You don’t want to make them feel like you’re actively pushing them away.

So, how’s the new exhibition going? You mentioned you were going to start working on it again after the holidays. Oh, it’s going very well, thank you. I’ve been spending a lot of time in the studio lately. I even got a few new pieces in. It’s interesting how inspiration comes at the most unexpected times. I was actually thinking about you the other day—remember that time we went to that art gallery in London? You were so excited about that abstract piece, weren’t you? Oh yes, I remember. I was completely gobsmacked. I couldn’t believe how the colors just seemed to move. I’ve been meaning to go back to that gallery again. I think they had an exhibition on modern art recently. Oh, I saw it. It was fantastic. A lot of young artists showcased their work there. It reminded me of how passionate you were about art when you were younger. I remember you used to sketch all the time at home, even when you were just a student. I still do, actually. It helps me get through university, honestly. I find that sketching or painting in between lectures helps me focus. It’s also why I’ve started taking some art courses on the side. That’s wonderful. I think it’s important to pursue your interests, no matter how small they seem. You know, I was in a similar position when I was your age. I studied art at university, and it’s what led me here—being an artist, working with galleries, and even traveling to different places to exhibit my work. That’s amazing. I’ve been thinking about traveling more after graduation. Maybe even abroad. I’ve got a few ideas for a trip to the Mediterranean, but I’m not sure yet. You should take the chance. I’ve been to Greece, Italy, and Spain, and they’re all so inspiring for an artist. The landscapes, the culture, the history—it all influences your work. Travel broadens the mind, as they say. I hope to do that soon. I’ve been saving up, and with the money I’ve got from part-time work, I think it’s possible. I also want to visit some of the art museums in those places. I think it would help me grow as an artist. That’s a great plan.

So, do you ever find it weird that we're still eating before the gym? I mean, it's like... we’re supposed to be healthy, right? I know, I mean, it’s not like we’re going to the gym for a snack break. But honestly, I think it’s just habit. I’ve been doing it for so long, I don’t even think about it anymore. Yeah, I guess. I mean, I remember when I was younger, I used to do it too. But now, I just feel like it’s such a waste. You eat, then you go and burn it off. What’s the point? Exactly! It’s like the gym is just a punishment for eating. Or maybe it’s just a way to feel like you’re doing something for yourself. Or maybe it’s about the ritual. The whole breakfast, then the gym thing. Like, you can’t be healthy without it. And honestly, I think it’s a bit of a myth. I mean, I’ve seen people who don’t do that and are perfectly fine. Yeah, but I think for some people, it’s more about the feeling of control. Like, if you eat a little, then you can work out – it’s a way to feel in charge of your body. I can see that. It’s kind of like the old “I eat, I exercise” thing. But I wonder if it’s just a cultural thing. Like, in the UK, we’re so into fitness, and we’re constantly told to eat less and move more. It’s like a package deal. I mean, I think there's some truth to that. It’s not just about being fit – it’s about how we define ourselves. If you’re not eating the right things or not exercising, you’re not disciplined. You’re not taking control. I guess. But it’s also funny how, as women, we’re always being told to eat less. We’re not even allowed to be hungry. Oh, absolutely. It’s such a huge part of the sexism in our culture. Women are constantly undermined by the idea that their bodies are something to control, something to be disciplined. And it’s not just about fitness – it’s about how we’re judged on our appearance. Exactly. So I think it’s a bit of a cycle.

So, do you remember that time we had that power cut last winter? I was in the middle of making a cup of tea and then— poof —everything went dark. Oh, I remember that! You were shouting, “Where’s the light?” like you’d been burgled or something. It was ridiculous. I was so upset I actually went outside with a torch and started looking for the fuse box in the garden. You were joking, weren’t you? You didn’t even have a torch. I did! I had one of those old-fashioned torches from the 90s. I found it in the shed and brought it in, thinking I was being all clever. And then what happened? Did the lights come back on? No, actually, they didn’t for quite a while. I was sitting there in the dark with a torch in my hand, looking like some kind of mad scientist, and then I heard a shout from the kitchen. Was it you? No, it was Adrian. He’d gone to check on the hob, and he came back shouting, “It’s gone!” “It’s gone?” What did he mean? He meant the power was back. He was so excited, he started dancing around the kitchen like it was a party. Oh, that’s Adrian. He’s always been a bit dramatic. I know, but it was funny. After that, I thought it would be a good idea to invest in a better kettle. You know, one that doesn’t require electricity. A manual kettle? You’ve got to be kidding me. No, a  stove-top  kettle, like the ones my mother used to have. You pour water in, put it on the hob, and wait. It’s so simple. I tried it once, and it was honestly terrifying. You mean the water boiling? No, the fact that I had to stand there, holding a kettle, waiting for it to boil, with the cat staring at me like I was about to murder it. That’s the spirit, love. You’ve got to stay grounded. I know, I know. But I think I’ve grown out of those kinds of things. I mean, I’ve got a PhD, for goodness’ sake. Yes, but you still have that little cat watching you like a hawk. That’s right. I think she’s been in the house longer than I have.

Mum, do you think we can go to the beach tomorrow? I really want to go. Oh, I was just thinking about that. It’s going to be a perfect day for the beach, isn’t it? The sun’s shining, and the sea’s calm. Yeah, I saw the forecast online. It said it’s going to be warm and sunny all day. I can’t wait to jump in the water. I remember when I was your age, I used to go to the beach every single summer. You’d never get tired of the waves. Yeah, I guess it’s just different now. I don’t think I’ve been to the beach in like, forever. I’ve been too busy with school. Well, this is your chance to get some fresh air and have fun. You should take your friends too, maybe? It’ll be more fun with company. I was thinking about inviting Emily and Lucy. They’re coming to visit this week anyway. We can all go together. That sounds great. I’d love to meet them. I’ve heard a lot about your friends from your mum. Oh, they’re lovely. Emily’s got a great sense of humour, and Lucy loves baking – she’s been making these amazing cakes for our family meetings. Yeah, she’s amazing. She even made a cake for my birthday last year. It was shaped like a unicorn. A unicorn cake? That sounds like something a child would make. Well, it was a unicorn, and she put glitter on it. It looked like a magical desert. I can imagine. You girls are always having such creative ideas. I think it’s a good idea to take your friends to the beach. It’ll give you a chance to catch up and enjoy some time together. I’m excited! I can’t wait to spend the day at the beach. I think I’ll bring my sunhat and some flip-flops. We can all wear matching swimwear. Matching swimwear? That’s a good idea. It’ll make the whole group look like a team. I’ll make sure to go to the shop and get some ice cream for everyone. It’s going to be a lovely day, I’m sure of it. Yeah, I think it’s going to be the best day ever. I can’t wait to see all my friends again.

I can't believe we just watched  10 Things I Hate About You . It was so cheesy, but I mean, it was kind of fun. Yeah, I know, right? I mean, it's not exactly a deep film, but it was a good laugh. And I loved how they turned the whole  The Taming of the Shrew  thing into a modern romance. I know, but I still can’t get over how much the actors looked like they were pulling it off. Especially when Patrick was doing the Shakespearean quotes. Oh, I saw that. It was so funny. I mean, it was awkward at first, but then it made sense. It was like they were trying to make a modern version of a classic, but it didn’t quite work. Yeah, but I think it was meant to be a bit of a comedy. I mean, if they had just done a straight adaptation, it would have been even worse. True. But still, the whole  10 things  thing was so over the top. I mean, how do you hate  ten  things about someone? It’s like they were trying to make a list of every single flaw. Exactly! And then at the end, when everything just magically worked out, it felt so unrealistic. Like, why didn’t they just go out and be honest from the beginning? I know, right? But maybe that’s what makes it so entertaining. It’s a romantic comedy, so it’s supposed to be ridiculous. I guess. Anyway, I’m just glad we finally watched it. I was so nervous about it. I thought it would be such a terrible movie. Me too! I was like, “I don’t know if I can handle this.” But honestly, it was better than I expected. Yeah, and I think it’s kind of a classic. Like, it’s one of those movies people keep rewatching just for the quotes. Definitely. I mean, who doesn't love “ I'm not a bad guy, I just don't like you ”? Exactly! It’s so iconic. I think we should definitely watch it again sometime. Maybe before our trip to London. You’re right. It’s a good way to unwind before the trip. I mean, we’ve got a few days planned—visiting the Tower of London, maybe going to a museum, and eating at that new café that’s supposed to be amazing.

So, do you know, I’ve been on Facebook a lot lately. I was just looking at old photos and... Well, I saw one of you, Speaker_2, when you were a child, with a little red coat and a bonnet. Looked like a proper little lady. Oh, you’re not wrong. I used to be the picture of a proper little lady. Though I don’t think I looked like that when I was in a bonnet, I swear. I was more of a tomboy. Especially when I was growing up in Harrow. Had to be the one to climb the tree in the back garden even though I was supposed to be learning my times tables. You were always the adventurous one, weren’t you? I remember hearing stories about how you used to sneak off to the park and play with the local kids even though your parents said you were too young. They nearly had a fit when you came home covered in mud with a stick in your hand. Yeah, and you didn’t even have a proper coat. Just a ratty sweater and a pair of trousers that had holes in them. I think it was the first time I ever saw someone dress like that and not be in trouble. You were always the one who got away with it. Oh, I was a fairly sneaky character, I’ll admit. But I had a good reason. I did have chicken pox for a while. And I don’t think I’d have survived it if someone hadn’t kept me indoors. I remember my mum saying that if I had gone out, I’d have ended up with a red face and a fever for weeks. And I  would  have gone out. I was determined to be like the other kids. Oh, you were always a bit of a rebel. But that was you. I mean, if you wanted to play with the other kids, who was I to stop you? Though I do think you were the only one who could manage to get away with all that. I think your rebellion started early. I remember hearing you talk about religion as a child. You used to say that you didn’t believe in the church, but you did believe in something. You just didn’t know what. And then one day, you suddenly did.

I just got a text from my cousin in Germany, and she’s talking about how her accent has changed since she’s been living there for five years. I’m like,  “You’re still a Brit, aren’t you?”  She said, “No, I’ve got a German accent now!” I laughed so hard, I almost spilled my wine. Oh, I know what she means. I used to be from Southport, and when I first moved to London, I used to say “chips” instead of “crisps,” and everyone would laugh at me. But now I just say “crisps” even when I’m back home. It’s weird, isn’t it? Yeah, I remember when I first went to London from Ashford. I had this massive accent, and I kept saying things like “I’m gonna go an’ get me a coffee!” and everyone looked at me like I was from another planet. I think I even got a bit of a laugh out of it, to be honest. I still have a strong accent, though, even after living in London for three years. I don’t think I’ve ever really lost it. My boss even jokes that I’m like a  “Kentish knight”  who never really left the countryside. That’s not entirely fair. I’ve been in Faversham my whole life, and I still use the word “‘ere” at the start of every sentence. I think it’s just how we are. Yeah, I can definitely tell where you’re from by the way you speak. It’s like a little Kentish fingerprint. I remember when my parents moved to Kemsing from somewhere else, and the locals just looked at them like they were aliens. I was like that too. I moved to London for work, and I found myself saying “biscuit” instead of “cookie” for years. I think I still say “biscuit” when I’m in London, even though I’ve been there for over a decade. It’s funny, isn’t it? No matter where you go, your accent is like a little part of you that you can’t shake. It’s like your identity. I think it’s more than just a way of speaking—it’s a part of who you are. Exactly. I can’t imagine ever speaking without that little  “‘ere”  at the start of everything. It’s just like,  “This is me.

So, how’s the kitchen going? I heard you’ve been experimenting with some new recipes lately. It’s been a bit of a rollercoaster. I’ve been trying to get into this new genre of fusion cuisine—like combining British and Mediterranean flavors. It’s been challenging, but I think I’m starting to get the hang of it. That sounds interesting. I’ve been into a lot of indie bands lately. Do you ever listen to music when you’re cooking? All the time! I actually have a playlist for every type of dish. The beat helps me get into the rhythm of chopping and stirring. I even have a drum track for when I’m making something that requires a bit of flair, like a stir-fry. That’s a cool idea. I’ve been into some drum and bass lately. I’m trying to get better at playing the drums myself. Do you play? Yeah, I do! I’ve been taking lessons for a few months now. It’s not perfect, but I’m getting there. I actually joined a local band a few weeks ago, and we’re doing some gigs in the area. That’s awesome! I’ve been thinking about getting an internship in the music industry. Have you got any advice? Definitely! I’d say start small—volunteer at a local venue or help out with a music event. Networking is huge in this field. You never know who you might meet that could open doors for you. That makes sense. I’ve been looking into a few internships, but I’m a bit nervous about the application process. Don’t be! You’ve got the skills and passion. Just take it step by step. And don’t forget to keep practicing your drumming. You never know when you might need that extra edge. Thanks, man. I’ll keep that in mind. Oh, by the way, have you heard the new album by that indie band we both like? Yeah, I did! It’s really good. I think they’re doing something different with their sound this time. It’s a bit more experimental, but I like it. I’m excited to check it out. Let me know if you want to go to a gig or something. I’d love to go with you. I’d like that. Maybe we can catch one of their shows in Exeter.

So, do you know what’s on your schedule for tomorrow, Love? I know it’s a school day, but I was thinking maybe we could do something fun after? Yeah, I guess so. I was thinking about going to the park with some friends. But I’m not sure if my phone’s going to work properly. I think I dropped it in the puddle yesterday. Oh no! That’s not good. Did you manage to get it out? I did, but it’s been acting up ever since. It keeps crashing when I try to open apps. I can’t even listen to my favourite radio station without it freezing. That’s not great. You know what you could do? Try to get it fixed at the shop. They usually do a quick check-up for free if it’s under warranty. But if not, maybe you could just wait until the weekend when you can actually relax and not worry about it. Yeah, you’re right. I’ll see what happens. But I was also thinking about the summer holiday—do you know when you’re going? I’m still waiting for a confirmation from the school. It’s all about the trips they’re planning. I think it’s going to be a few weeks from now. I’m hoping it’s to somewhere with a bit of natural beauty, like Durham or maybe even the Lake District. That sounds cool. I’d love to see the countryside again. I’ve been stuck in Newcastle for so long. All the noise and rush of the city. I can barely sleep anymore. I know what you mean. That’s why I always bring a sleeping bag when I go out. I’ve even started using a pillow from the office just to get some decent rest. It’s not ideal, but better than nothing. Yeah, I’ve thought about that. But I’m not sure if I can bring one. My school just handed me a shopping list, and it was all about snacks and drinks. No mention of sleeping bags or anything like that. Well, maybe you can always ask the teachers. I mean, you are in full-time education, right? They must have something for you. Yeah, I guess. I’ll see if I can talk to them. But I’m really not looking forward to the weekend.

So, how’s the new flat? I heard you moved in a few weeks ago. How’s it going? It’s going well, thanks. It’s a bit of a hassle getting used to the flat, but it’s nice and quiet. I’ve got a bit of a problem with the heating though—sometimes it doesn’t work properly. Not sure if it’s the boiler or something else. Aww, that’s annoying. I had a similar issue with my old flat. It’s just so inconvenient. You ever think about getting a smart thermostat or something? I was thinking about it. Maybe I’ll try to get one before winter comes. I’ve heard they’re quite reliable now. My friend from uni mentioned they fixed his heating problem with one. Anyway, how are you? You’ve been pretty quiet since you moved to Sussex. Yeah, I’ve been busy settling in, and I’ve been trying to get my head around the cost of living here. Rent is a lot higher, even though I’m not in the city. I’m still trying to adjust my budget, and I haven’t even started thinking about buying a car yet. I know what you mean. I’ve been trying to live frugally, but it’s got to be tough. My salary is okay, but I’m still figuring out how to manage the bills. You know, I was thinking about taking on some freelance work to make a bit extra. Maybe something with my old job? Or even teaching online? That could work. I’ve been doing a bit of freelance translation work on the side, and it’s helping me make a bit more money. Though, honestly, it’s about the same as my main job. I just need to find something that gives me a bit more stability. I know what you mean. It’s tough, but I guess that’s life for us. Speaking of life, how’s everything going with your family? Still planning on getting married? Yeah, I am. I’ve been talking to my partner about it, and we’re planning to get married next year. We’ve got a little budget saved up, and we’re going to look for a place to live together by then. That’s great! I’m so happy for you. You two have been together for a while now, right?

I just got a call from my sister. She's been really down lately. She's been dealing with some health issues, and I think she's been struggling more than she lets on. Oh no, I’m sorry to hear that. How is she? She’s been in and out of the hospital, and it’s been tough on the whole family. She's got cancer, and it’s not looking good. I just wish there was more we could do for her. That sounds really hard. I can’t imagine what you’re going through. Have you spoken to the doctors yet about the next steps? We have, but the options are limited. She’s in remission now, but it came back stronger this time. The doctors said it’s aggressive, and the treatment isn’t working as well as before. That must be so frustrating. How is she coping emotionally? She’s trying her best, but she’s not the same as she used to be. She’s been so tired, and she doesn’t want to burden us with her worries. We all try to be strong for her, but honestly, it’s wearing us out. I can only imagine. I’ve been thinking about my own mother lately. She’s been dealing with something similar, and I know how hard it is to watch someone you love struggle. Have you thought about getting some support? We have, but it’s hard to find the right kind of help. We’ve been to a few counseling sessions, but it’s not enough. Some days, I just feel like I can’t handle it all. You’re not alone in feeling that way. I’m sure there are support groups and other people who have been through similar experiences. Maybe you could reach out to them. I know, but it’s hard to take the first step. I keep thinking about how things used to be. She used to be so vibrant and full of life, and now it’s like a shadow of who she was. I know. I’ve seen how much she meant to the family, and I can only imagine how hard this is for all of you. I’m here if you need anything, you know that. Thank you. It means a lot. I’m just trying to stay positive, but it’s not easy.

Alright, let’s just see if we can get through this meal without anyone getting too distracted. I’ve got a few things on my mind, especially about the kids’ future. Yeah, I know. I was thinking about apprenticeships too. I mean, it’s not like university is the only way to go, right? I’ve heard some people say it’s better to get on the job and learn a trade. Absolutely. I’ve got a cousin who started an apprenticeship in engineering and now he’s running his own workshop. It’s pretty impressive. But, honestly, it’s not for everyone. Some kids just don’t have the maturity for it. I mean, I guess that’s what’s been on my mind too. I’m not sure what I want to do after school. I like football, and I think I could be a good player, but I’ve also been thinking about starting my own business. I’ve been messing around with some ideas online. That’s a fair point. You’ve got a lot of potential, but it’s important to think about what you’re really passionate about. Do you have any idea what kind of business you might want to start? Not really, to be honest. I’ve been looking into some mobile apps, like – I don’t know – maybe something related to sports? Or maybe something like tutoring? I’m not sure. You know what? I think you should talk to your teachers. They’ve got experience with things like this. Maybe even my dad? He runs his own business, and he’s always saying how it’s better to start small and build up. Yeah, and you know what about football? I mean, if you’re serious about playing, there are some really good coaches in the area. I know there’s a new tennis and football academy near here. You could do both, like combine your interest in sport with something else. That’s a good idea. It’s not like you can’t have a dual focus. I remember when I was a kid, I played cricket and did some academies too. It kept me busy and gave me a good head start. So, are you saying I should try applying for the football coaching programme? I mean, it’s not like I’m not interested in it. I’ve been watching a lot of matches on YouTube.

So, do you think we’ll get to Lancaster on time? I’ve been trying to get a signal on my phone all the way from Aylesbury, and it’s been like a ghost town out here. Yeah, honestly, I don’t know. It’s been like a nightmare trying to get on the train. I had to wait for an hour at Lincoln Station because the previous train was delayed for a missing carriage or something. I just hope we don’t end up missing the last one. Oh no! That’s not good. I was looking forward to getting to the station early enough to get a good seat and maybe grab a bite to eat before we start the journey. I was thinking about fish and chips—do you fancy that later? The last time I had it, it was so good, but I almost lost the whole thing in a cockle disaster. Oh, you’re not going to tell me you still have that story, are you? I remember the time you tried to eat a cockle and it ended up in your lap. I still laugh about it. I think it was a Christmas visit to the coast, wasn’t it? Yep, and I thought I’d found the perfect coastal town—just the kind of place I’d like to visit for my dissertation research. I was going to study the local dialects and how they’ve evolved over time, especially in places that have strong coastal communities. That sounds interesting. I’d love to hear more about that when we get there. I’m actually thinking of doing something similar for my masters. I’ve had the idea for a while, but I’ve been putting it off because I’m still trying to figure out how to structure it. That’s good, you know. It’s one of the things I love about studying languages—it’s like you get to explore so many different aspects of people and places. I mean, even the way people talk can tell you so much about their history and the influences they’ve had over the years. I know, right? My family is from Lincoln, and I grew up hearing a lot of different accents and dialects in the area. My mum’s from the north, and my dad’s from the south. It’s always been interesting to hear how they mix their speech sometimes.

So, do you know what’s been going on with the band we used to follow? I feel like they’ve gone off the rails a bit. Yeah, I know, they’ve been super busy with their new album. I heard they’ve been working with some really big producers. But I also heard some weird stuff about them splitting up? Oh no, really? I thought they were still together. I mean, they’ve been doing a lot of festivals recently, but maybe they’re just pulling back? I think it’s more than that. I read somewhere that the lead singer had some issues with addiction. I mean, I don’t know the details, but it’s been rumoured they had some kind of fall out with the rest of the band. That’s sad. I can’t imagine how that would feel. I mean, they used to be the biggest thing in the whole Yorkshire scene. You know, back when we were in school, they were like the cool thing to be into. Yeah, I remember when they first started. It’s weird. I still think they’re really talented, though. I mean, don’t get me wrong, their music was always a bit edgy, but there was something about their live shows that made you feel like you were part of something bigger. Like, they had this energy that you couldn’t ignore. Yeah, I miss that energy. I guess it’s part of why I still listen to their older stuff. I just hope they come back together one day. It would be cool to see them play again. I’d love that. I mean, I’m not sure if I’d go to a show anymore, but if they did a reunion tour, I’d definitely try to make it. It’s just… you know, I sort of miss the days when we were all just kids, and everything felt like it was possible. Yeah, I know what you mean. It’s funny how time flies. Alright, do you two remember what we were talking about earlier? About the CBeebies pantomime? Oh yes! We were talking about whether we should take the kids to see it this summer. So, do you think we should actually move out of this flat? I mean, it's been a year now, and honestly, I’m starting to feel like we’re just going in circles. You’re not going in circles, you’re just… being realistic. I mean, it’s not that bad, is it? I like the location, and the rent’s not terrible. I agree with Alistair. So, do you remember when we were kids and we used to play with those plastic soldiers? I think I still have mine in a box somewhere. I can't say I do, but I remember we used to have these little plastic tanks and we’d set up battlefields in the garden. It was all about who could win the most battles. Oh, I had that same set! I remember my brother used to pretend he was a general, and I was his assistant. We used to argue over who got to be the leader. That sounds familiar. I think my dad used to get really into it, and he’d make up the most ridiculous battle strategies. I still remember him once trying to convince me that the best way to win was to just throw the soldiers at the enemy. Oh, I bet he had a point, in a way. It was all about strategy and tactics, even if it was just for fun. Yeah, but I think the real fun was when we’d argue over who got to pick the toys first. I always had to choose the best one, and my brother would just take whatever was left. That’s probably why we always ended up in fights. But it was funny in a way – we were just kids, trying to be serious about our toys. I don’t know, I think those days were the best. You don’t have the pressures of work or life, just the simple joy of play. Definitely. I can’t help but think about the way we used to talk too. I mean, we used to make up our own dialects and slang, just like we do now. Oh, I remember that. We used to say things like “chuffed” and “knackered” all the time, even though we didn’t really know what they meant. That’s true. I think it was a way to feel like we were part of something bigger, like we had our own language. It’s funny how those things stay with you. I still use some of those words today, even though I’m an accountant now. Yeah, I still do too. It’s like our childhood language – it’s part of who we are. That’s probably why I’ve always been interested in dialects. I mean, I’ve worked in roles where I had to deal with people from all over the country, and it’s fascinating how different people speak.

So, did you have a good time in Spain, Dad? I mean, you said it was a week away, but I didn’t really get the full story yet. Oh, it was absolutely brilliant, love. We had a bit of a whirlwind trip, but it was all worth it. Yeah, it was a good one. We basically did all the main attractions. You know, the beach, the tapas, the flamenco, and even a few nights in a reasonable hotel. Wait, you stayed in a hotel? That’s a big step up from the last time you went on holiday, wasn’t it? Oh, come on, it’s not like I’ve never stayed in a proper hotel before. I just didn’t think I’d get to Spain and not have to sleep in a caravan or something. Wait, you stayed in a caravan? That’s not a hotel. No, no, no, not at all. We stayed in a few different places, but the one we liked the most was this little guesthouse in Granada. It had a great view and the owner was a real character. Yeah, and we got to meet a few local people. One of them was a retired teacher who spoke excellent English and told us all these amazing stories about the history of the city. That sounds like a real trip. What kind of food did you eat? Oh, the food was amazing. We ate so much. Spanish tapas, paella, chorizo, and that incredible seafood at a little place near the beach. Wait, you ate seafood? I thought you didn’t like it. Oh, I do like it. I just didn’t think I’d be able to have it in Spain. Turns out, it was even better than I imagined. You know, I was thinking about that the other day. I remember when you were a kid, you used to complain about the school dinners. You said they were the worst. Oh, I said that because they were  terrible . I remember once I had a chicken nugget that looked like it had been sitting in a box for two weeks. That’s not fair, Dad. You’re exaggerating. No, I’m not. I remember one time I asked for a salad, and they gave me a piece of broccoli with a sauce that tasted like old cod. You really did hate school dinners, didn’t you?

So, do you know what’s up with the fridge? It’s been making this weird noise all night. Like,  rrrrrrr  every now and then. I’ve checked the door, it’s not stuck, and the shelves are all fine. Hmm, maybe it’s the compressor? I’ve heard that happens with older fridges. But I thought we had a new one last year? Or was that just a rental? Oh, it was a rental. We had it for like three months and then we just moved out and left it. So, I guess it’s not even ours anymore. Maybe it’s just the age of the fridge, or the fact that we left it on all the time. Yeah, I remember telling Anna last week that we need to get a new one. But she said we should just patch it up for now. I don’t know, it’s getting worse. Well, maybe we should check if it’s still under warranty. If we can, we could take it to a repair shop. Or maybe even get a second opinion. I’m not sure I want to spend money on a fridge that might break again. What if we just buy a new one? I mean, it’s only a few hundred pounds. We can’t be living with a fridge that’s making that noise all night. Yeah, I agree. But maybe we should get the landlord’s opinion first? I mean, they’re the ones who let it to us. They might not want to pay for repairs. That’s a good point. But then again, if it’s their fault, maybe they should handle it. I mean, we’re just tenants. We don’t own the place. I know, but we’re not exactly in the best position. I mean, if we take it to a repair shop, they might say it’s too old. And if it’s not covered by warranty, we might end up paying for it all ourselves. I know. I just don’t want to be up at 3 a.m. trying to sleep with that noise. It’s annoying. Yeah, I can’t even sleep properly with that. I told my sister about it the other day, and she said it’s like a haunted fridge. Ha, that’s a good one. But seriously, what if we just get a new fridge?

So, do you think we’ll actually make it to the airport on time? I mean, it’s only like a 20-minute drive from here, but with the traffic, who knows. I don’t know, honestly. I tried using Google Maps before I left, and it said it’d take 18 minutes, but then I got stuck behind a lorry for ten minutes. You don’t even know what’s going on on the roads sometimes. Yeah, I was in the same boat. I used to rely on my Satnav so much when I was working in the city. I’d just follow the directions, and everything was fine. But then the day I got stuck in a gridlock that lasted an hour, I realized I should probably not trust it completely. I still use my phone for directions, but I’ve learned to take a mental map. My wife says I’m a bit of a lost cause, but I’m pretty sure I’ve got a better sense of direction than most people, even if I do get a bit flustered. That’s the thing, isn’t it? I mean, if we’re not careful, we might end up in a place we’ve never been before, and then we have to figure out how to get back. I remember once I got turned around in Cambridge and ended up in a totally different part of the city. It took me like an hour to find my way back. That sounds familiar. I was in Liverpool once and my Satnav told me to take a turn that didn’t exist. I was literally walking down a street that didn’t have a name, and I thought I had to be in the wrong country. That’s the thing with the apps, though. They’re so much better now than they used to be. I mean, I can’t imagine navigating without them now. I just wish they didn’t make you feel so useless when they’re wrong. I’ve heard people say the same thing. There was a time when you just had to know your way around, but now it’s all about the apps. Even my grandkids use them more than I do. That’s true. I remember my dad used to tell me stories about how he used to map out his routes manually.

So, do you think we should bring some kind of sun protection with us? I mean, it’s Sweden, but the sun’s been really strong today, and I don’t want to get burnt after all that work in the garden. I know what you mean. I actually brought a bottle of sun cream just in case. I’ve got one with SPF 30, which I think is pretty high. But I also heard that some people in the garden use a kind of oil or something to protect their skin. Yeah, and I’ve heard that some of the garden staff use a natural oil made from plants. I think it’s called aloe vera or something like that. It’s supposed to help with sunburns and also nourish the skin. Interesting. I’ve never used anything like that before. I just use regular sun cream, but maybe I should try it. I mean, I’ve been working in the garden a lot, and my skin’s been getting pretty dry. Yeah, I’ve noticed that too. It’s not just the sun, it’s the combination of being out in the elements, moving around, and the plants themselves. They can be pretty drying. Exactly. And it’s not just about the sun. Even if it’s cloudy, you can still get UV exposure. I’ve read that even on overcast days, you can still get sunburned. So it’s important to protect your skin all year round. I’ve heard that too. It’s one of those things that people don’t take seriously until they get burned. I’ve got a friend who got really bad sunburn last summer and it took weeks to recover. Oh no, that sounds awful. I hope you’re okay. I know that the gardens here in Stockholm have some amazing plants, but I do worry about the sun. Maybe we should check if there are any shaded areas we can use while we’re working. That’s a good idea. I’ve heard that some of the newer garden beds have canopies or structures to provide shade. If we ask the garden staff, they might be able to direct us to those areas. I’ll do that. I’d rather work in the shade than risk getting sunburned. Speaking of which, I’ve been wondering—do you think plants can actually help with your overall health?

I just can’t get over how different my accent is from my parents. I mean, it’s like I’m from a completely different part of the country, even though I was born in Kent. You know, I can hear that difference too. You sound more like someone from the South East, whereas your mum and dad have that more traditional London accent. It’s funny how accents can change over time. Yeah, I’ve noticed that too. My accent is more of a mix, like Harlow and East London. I don’t know if it’s because I grew up in a different area or just because of the way people speak now. I don’t think I have an accent at all. I mean, I was born in Chatham, and I still sound like I’m from Chatham. It’s not like the way people in London or Manchester speak. It’s just plain. I mean, I suppose I do sound a bit like the way people speak on TV, like in those reality shows. It’s like I’ve been influenced by the media more than my parents. I think that’s a fair point. TV and the internet have such a big impact on how we speak now. I remember when I was younger, everyone had a much stronger regional accent, but now people speak more like they’re trying to be understood by everyone. It’s also funny because I’ve heard you speak and sometimes I can’t even tell where you’re from. It’s like you’re just a mix of different places. That’s not me. I sound like I’m from a village where no one ever spoke properly. I mean, I grew up in a place where people just talked the way they always have. No need for fancy words. I think that’s what makes us so different. I mean, I’m from the same area as you, Chatham, but I just have this strange way of speaking. Maybe it’s because you’ve been exposed to more different dialects. Like, I know you’ve been to London a few times, right? That must have influenced you somehow. I think it’s also because of the way we’re raised. My mum always wanted me to speak properly, so I think she influenced me in that way. I don’t know, I just feel like I have to speak more clearly than some people.

Alright, do you want some of this baked Alaska? I made it for the Halloween party, and it’s still warm. Oh, is that the one with the ice cream and the sponge? Yeah, exactly. I thought it would be a nice treat. But it’s kind of a bit of a mess, honestly. It took me ages to get the ice cream to freeze properly before I could put the sponge on top. It’s mostly for the Halloween party, but I thought I’d make it today so it’s ready. Anyway, I also made some cheesy gratin. I don’t even know what a ritual is. I mean, I know it’s something you do on purpose, but I don’t really know. I mean, is it like a tradition? Or is it like... something you do for fun? It’s a tradition, sort of. It’s something that brings people together. I think that’s why I still do it. It’s part of who I am. Hmm. I guess I don’t really have that. I mean, I do things like... I don’t know. I just cook what I go out and buy. If I want to cook, I just do. Well, I think we all have our own ways of doing things. It’s just how we express ourselves. Yeah, I guess.

So, do you know what’s happening with the refuse collection this week? I was just wondering if they’re going to be on time or not. I’ve been leaving the bins out all week, and I’m starting to think they’ve forgotten about us. Honestly, I can’t tell you. I think they’re running behind schedule. I got an email from the council saying there's a delay due to a backlog. It’s funny how different places handle waste. I’ve never been to Japan, but I’ve heard a lot about it from friends who’ve lived there. I’d love to visit and maybe even take some flying lessons while I’m there. I’ve always wanted to fly a plane. Flying lessons? That sounds amazing. I’ve been thinking about it too. I told my kids I wanted to get a pilot’s license, but they just laughed at me. I figure if I can’t do it now, when will I? I’ve got the time and the money, so maybe I should just start learning.

I can't believe I missed the last game. I was just walking in the door and saw the board and thought, "Oh no, I’ve missed the whole thing." You’re lucky you didn’t miss the final move. You’ve got that triple word score. I know, I know. But I couldn’t think of anything else. I was just trying to remember if there was a  Q  left. There’s a  Q  left, but I think you should’ve gone for  quinoa  instead. It’s a real word, and it’s got a  Q  and an  I .  Quinoa  is a bit of a stretch for some people. I mean, not everyone knows what it is. Yeah, I mean, I’ve heard of it, but I’ve never actually tried it. It’s a superfood, though. I read about it in one of those magazines that come with the coffee. You mean the ones that have all those articles about plants and flowers? Yeah, the ones that made me want to grow a garden just to read about it. I’ve thought about doing that. My flatmate’s got a balcony, and I’ve been thinking about growing some herbs. That’s a good idea. Maybe you could grow some  quinoa  too. It’s easy, right? Not really. You know, I remember reading that  quinoa  is one of those words that comes from the Quechua language. It’s like, the people who live in the Andes. That’s interesting. I always thought it was from somewhere else. I think it’s got that  Q  sound, which is pretty rare in English. It’s like  quill  or  queue . And the spelling is even trickier. You’ve got to remember that it’s  quinoa , not  quinooa  or  quinoa . I kind of like that. It’s like it’s trying to be a bit of a tough word to spell. Yeah, it’s like the language is giving you a little challenge.

I've been thinking a lot lately, you know, about how things have changed since I was a boy. It’s like the world’s gone mad, isn’t it? Oh, I know what you mean. I remember when we had the post-war housing boom and everything was so different. Back then, people didn’t worry about things like today—no internet, no smartphones, just the basic needs. Yeah, but I think the biggest change is how people are now. It’s all about getting ahead, getting money, and moving up. Back in my day, we didn’t think about that too much. We just worked hard and made do with what we had. You’re right about that. I still remember my father saying, “A roof over your head and food on the table is what matters.” But now, people are constantly chasing success. It’s like they’ve forgotten what it means to live simply. And with all this change, there’s also more pressure on people, especially the young ones. I was talking to my son the other day—his job’s not secure, and he’s got kids of his own now. It’s like he’s got to be twice as smart as we were to make ends meet. He’s got a good head on his shoulders though. He’s trying, and I know he’s got a good heart. But it’s not enough, is it? You’ve got to have the right connections, the right education, the right opportunities. Yes, and that’s the problem, isn’t it? You can be smart, hardworking, and still be left behind. I mean, I had a colleague at work who was a brilliant man—always came up with ideas, but he didn’t have the right connections. He ended up leaving the country because there was no future here. That’s heartbreaking. I think the real tragedy is that people are being pushed further and further down. And it’s not just the young ones. I see it in my own age group too. You’ve got people who are retired, but they can’t afford to live on their pensions. It’s all so unfair. We worked hard, paid our taxes, and now we’re left picking up the pieces. I think the system is broken, and it’s not going to fix itself.

So, did you watch that episode of Shakespeare on TV last night? I tried to, but I kept falling asleep. Honestly, I didn’t even make it past the first act. It was like watching a play in a library with no one else around—too quiet, too slow. Yeah, I know what you mean. So how have you been? It's been a while since we last caught up. Honestly, I’ve been okay, just juggling work and life. I’ve had a few crazy days with the marketing campaign we’re running. So, do you know what’s happening with the new plants in the garden? I think it’s going to be a real mess if we don’t sort them out soon. Yeah, I know. I was thinking about it last night. Maybe we can try making a batch this weekend? Yeah, that sounds perfect. And maybe we can set up a little table by the window so we can enjoy it while we’re gardening. I think it’d be nice. Definitely. I’ve got this new recipe I found on the BBC Good Food Show. It’s pesto with a twist — they use walnuts instead of pine nuts, and it’s supposed to be more nutty.

So, how was your weekend, Rhys? I heard you had a few people round for dinner. Oh, it was great, Tom. We had a few of the lads from the football club over. Alright, do you know what’s happening this weekend? Your dad’s got a meeting with the church about the Christening, and I think they’re planning to do it at the same time as your birthday. So, do you think we should go to New York this year? I mean, it's been a while since we went on a proper holiday. I think it's a good idea. So, I've been trying to get my paperwork sorted for the thesis, but it's just not going smoothly. So, do you think we’ll ever get a dog, Lottie? I mean, it’s been ages since we talked about it. I think it’s about time, actually. It’s not just about us—it’s about the whole family.

So, do you know what’s up with the A&E? I swear it’s always full, like,  always . You can’t even get a seat unless you’re in a wheelchair or something. Yeah, I know. I was there last week with a friend who had a broken arm. Took like two hours just to get seen. And they didn’t even give him a cup of tea. A cup of tea? That’s the  minimum  they should give you. I mean, you’re in pain, you’re worried, and then you get a cold cup of water and a grim-faced nurse saying, “Right, let’s see what we can do.” Exactly. It’s like they don’t care. I mean, I got a sprained ankle and I had to wait for  hours  because they said they were “short-staffed.” What’s the point of having an A&E if they’re just going to ignore people? I don’t know. I think it’s just the way the system is. Like, everyone’s so busy, and there’s so many patients, and no one takes the time to actually care. I’ve heard that before. But it’s not just about the staff. I think it’s also about the way the system works. Like, they’re not trained to handle the volume, and they’re not given the resources. It’s like a never-ending cycle. Yeah, and then you have people like me who just get caught in the system because they’re not that bad. I had a minor injury, like a small cut, and I ended up being told I had to wait  two hours  for a bandage. It was ridiculous. I know, it’s just so frustrating. I’ve seen people with life-threatening injuries waiting for hours because the system is too busy. It’s not just a matter of being lazy—it’s about how things are set up. I don’t think people realise how bad it is. I mean, I know it’s a problem everywhere, but hearing about it from friends and family, it’s like the system is just broken. Yeah, and it’s not just in the UK. I’ve heard the same stories from people in other countries. It’s like a global issue. Still, I think people should be more aware of how bad it is.

Well, I've just made the tea, so I suppose we can start drinking it. Oh, thank you, Bill. That’s very kind of you. Yes, and it looks good. You’ve gone for the proper teabag this time, haven’t you? So, do you think we should go to the pub after dinner? I heard there's a new place opening up in Dereham. I’d love to, but I’m not sure if we can afford it.
