So, do you know, I’ve been thinking about the North East a lot lately. It’s like, even though I’m in Cambridge, I still feel like I’m from Sunderland. You know, that accent, that vibe, that whole way of speaking… it’s like a part of me that I can’t shake. I get that. I was born and bred in Birmingham, but I’ve spent a lot of time in the North. I mean, I went to university in Manchester, and I still feel like I’ve got that Northern edge to me. It’s in the way I talk, the way I think, the way I even dress. I can’t seem to escape it, no matter how far I travel. Yeah, I feel the same. I remember when I moved to London for my postgrad, and I thought I’d be the one who’d blend in, you know? But then I’d walk into a room and this guy would say “aye” or “laddie” and I’d just feel like I’d been caught out. It was like,  what’s wrong with me?  I don’t even know how I sound anymore. I’ve had that too. I still say “brolly” instead of “umbrella” and “luggage” instead of “bag.” It’s weird, isn’t it? You think you’ve left that part of your life behind, but it clings on like a bad habit. Exactly. And I think it’s not just the accents. It’s the way we dress, the way we talk about things. Like, I still have this thing for being overdressed for the weather. It’s like,  I’m about to go out and I need to look the part, even if it’s raining cats and dogs.  I love that! I mean, it’s kind of charming, isn’t it? I’ve always thought the North had this kind of rugged, understated elegance. Like, it’s not about being flashy, it’s about being real. And I think that’s what makes it so unique. Yeah, and I think that’s why I’ve always been drawn to music from the North. Bands like The Smiths, Pulp, maybe even early Oasis. There’s something about their music that just  gets  you. You know? It’s not just songs—it’s a feeling, a place, a way of life. I completely agree.

Grandpa, I heard you were talking about the new council plan on the telly. What do you think about it? Oh, I’m not sure, lad. I've been thinking about it a lot. You know, I remember when I was your age, the council used to make decisions that actually helped the community, not just the rich folks. But isn’t that what they say now? That they’re trying to help everyone? Oh, they say that, but you know what? It's all just window dressing. They're still pushing through the same old plans — more housing, more roads, more of everything. But where’s the care for the people who’ve been here all their lives? Like who? Like the old folks like me, or the ones who’ve lived in the area for generations. It's all about money and development. They’re just trying to make the place look better for the tourists and the new people coming in. But didn’t they say the new housing would help the homeless? Yeah, and that’s what they want you to think. But land is expensive now, and they’re not building proper homes — just shoddy little bungalows that will fall apart in a few years. And then what? You’re back to square one. I don’t know. It all sounds complicated. It is complicated, lad. But the important thing is to keep asking questions. Don’t let them talk you into anything. I’ve seen it happen before. People think they’re making things better, but in the end, it’s just more problems. What do you think about the new council leader? Well, I don’t know much about them. They seem young, and that’s a bad sign. You need someone with experience. Someone who understands the real issues — not just the shiny new projects. Like what kind of issues? Oh, you know — the schools, the hospitals, the roads, the pubs. The things that keep a place alive. If you don’t take care of those, you’re just building a ghost town. So you think the council is doing it wrong? I think they’re doing it the wrong way. They’re making decisions without listening to the people who live here. And that’s a big mistake. I guess I should start paying more attention. I never really thought about it before.

So, do you remember the last time we had a proper family meal like this? I think it was when the kids were still at home and we used to make a big fuss over dinner. Yeah, I remember. It was like a ritual. We’d all sit around the table, make a lot of noise, and argue about who got the bigger piece of meat. It was chaos, but in a good way. Honestly, I miss that. Now, with the toddler, it's just me trying to keep her from knocking things over and making sure the food doesn’t end up on the floor. Oh, I remember when I was a teacher and I had to teach table manners to my students. It was all about respect, not being too loud, and knowing when to speak. I used to say, "If you can’t say something nice, don’t say anything at all." That’s good advice, but I still think some of the old traditions are worth keeping. Like, not putting your fork in your mouth, and not talking with your mouth full. It’s just polite. Yeah, I mean, we all know that, but sometimes when you’re hungry, you just go on autopilot. I tried to teach my little brother that when I was growing up, but he just said, “It’s fine, Grandma doesn’t mind.” That’s exactly what I have to deal with. My toddler just says, “It’s fine, Mummy doesn’t mind,” and I just sigh. I’m not even sure what she means by that. It’s funny how the younger generation approaches things so differently. We grew up with strict rules, and now it’s all about being relaxed and having fun. I think it’s a good balance. You don’t want to be too strict, but you also want to have some structure. Especially when you’re hosting a family meal. I used to love the way we used to all sit together and talk, even if we were arguing about the football or something. Yeah, and that’s what I miss most. It used to be a chance to catch up with everyone, even if it was just about the weather or what we had for dinner. Now it’s more about the toddler and if she’s going to sleep soon. I’m sure she’ll be fine.

So, do you know what’s been on my mind all week? That Scottish referendum. I just can’t get it off my mind. I mean, I’m from Brighton, but I’ve got a cousin who lives in Glasgow, and he’s been pretty vocal about it. Yeah, I heard about that. I think the country’s got bigger issues than that, but I can see why people are passionate about it. I guess it’s about identity, you know? It’s not just about the economy or the constitution—it’s about what it means to be Scottish. But then again, I’ve got a colleague from Edinburgh who’s been saying it’s all about the EU and how Scotland would be better off outside of it. Yeah, I can see that argument. But I also heard some people say that staying in the UK is better for the NHS, the healthcare system, the education. Exactly. And with the economy in the state it’s in, I don’t know, it’s kind of a toss-up. But I still can’t shake the feeling that if it had gone through, it would have changed a lot for a lot of people. I suppose it would have. But I’m not sure it was the best way to settle it. I mean, it’s not like they could’ve just sat down and had a chat and come to an agreement. No, no, no. It’s a referendum, it’s supposed to be a democratic process. But I can’t help but think that it’s a bit of a symbolic gesture at this point. What’s the point of voting if the government isn’t going to take it seriously? I guess you’re right. But then again, it’s not just about the politics. It’s about the people. I mean, if you’re a Scottish person, and you’ve got a say in your own future, shouldn’t you be able to exercise that? That’s true. I don’t think I’d have been in favour of it, but I can understand why people would be. It’s just sad to see the whole country divided over it, you know? Yeah, it’s a shame. I’ve been thinking about my own life lately. I had a job interview last week, and it was interesting.

So, Dad, are we going to make a stop for lunch or are we just heading straight through? I thought we could do a quick stop at the supermarket on the way. It’s a bit of a drive, and I don’t fancy driving all the way to the city just for a sandwich. Yeah, I mean, I haven’t had proper food all day. I was teaching a session this morning and then got stuck in a meeting for an hour. That sounds exhausting. You should take more breaks, Aaron. I know, I know. It’s just the whole teaching thing. I get so caught up in the lesson plans and the students that I forget to look after myself. It’s easy to get into that rut. I remember when I was doing my A-levels, I used to skip meals just to save time. I still do that sometimes. I used to do that too, but now I try to make time for proper meals. I mean, I’m still in the early stages of my career, but I’d rather be healthy than tired. I agree. It’s not just about being healthy, it’s also about having enough energy for the day. You can’t teach – or work – properly if you’re constantly running on caffeine. Exactly. It’s like when you’re at home and you’re trying to work on your art, and you’re just so sleepy, you can’t even concentrate. That’s true. I think you need to have a proper routine, even if it’s just a few minutes of stretching or a light snack before you get into anything serious. Speaking of which, I had this idea for a new board game idea. It’s based on the concept of moving house, which I think would be a lot of fun. A board game based on moving house? That’s a bit of an unusual concept, but I can see how it could work. I mean, I’ve had to move house a few times, and it’s a bit of a chaotic process. Yeah, it’s like a huge puzzle. You’ve got the furniture, the boxes, the paperwork, and then you have to figure out where everything goes. It’s almost like a real-life game of Tetris. Exactly! So if you were to make a board game out of it, you’d have to think about all the different stages – packing, moving, unpacking, and settling in.

So, do you know how long we've been driving? Not sure, love. I’d say about an hour or so. I think it’s been over an hour. I’ve been checking the time on my phone. Yeah, I’ve been thinking the same. I’ve got a bad feeling about this. What do you mean? I think we might be going the wrong way. Are you sure? I’m not sure. I’ve been trying to remember the route. It’s been a while since I’ve driven this way. You know, I think the A66 goes through here. I remember seeing a sign for Cumbria earlier. Yeah, but we’re going towards the north, aren’t we? Maybe we are. I mean, I did drive through Carlisle a while back. Wait, Carlisle is in the north, right? So if we’re going that way, we’re on the right track. Unless we’re going to the wrong side of the motorway. That’s a possibility. I’ve had that happen before. You get on the motorway and then you’re not sure if you’re going east or west. That’s what I was thinking. I’ve been trying to find a sign that says ‘Cumbria’ or ‘Westmorland’ to confirm we’re on the right road. What’s the point of driving all this way if we get lost again? I know, love. I just don’t want to end up going back the way we came. I’d rather we just keep going for now. If we hit a town or something, we can check the map. Yeah, and maybe we can stop at a service station. I’ve got some money in my pocket. Right. I think we’re getting close to the next town. I can see some lights in the distance. Is that Carlisle? I don’t know. Maybe. Let’s keep going and see. Alright, let’s just go with it. If we’re wrong, we’ll find out soon enough. Yeah, I’m not going to panic. I’ve driven to the farm before. I just need to remember the way. You’ll get there. I’ve done it before. Just keep calm and take it one road at a time. That’s the spirit. Let’s just keep moving. Yeah, let’s not think too much. Just drive. And if we do get lost, we can always ask for directions.

So, do you know what’s for dinner tonight? I asked Sarah, and she just said, “Something like a roast, I suppose,” which is the same as every other night. I’m starting to wonder if she’s even trying anymore. You know, I wouldn’t say that. She’s just not the most enthusiastic cook. But she does know her way around a good roast. Though honestly, I’ve been thinking about getting a new recipe book. I got one last week from the library, and it’s full of interesting ideas. Maybe we could try something new this week, like a slow-cooked meat with some root vegetables? That sounds nice, but I’m not sure if we’re in the mood for a big meal. I’ve been thinking about going for a run this evening. It’s been a while since I last did. A bit of fresh air and exercise would do me good. That’s a good idea, Brian. You know, I used to run with the local group when I was still teaching. It was a great way to unwind after a long day. But since I’ve retired, I’ve not really kept it up. Maybe we could all go together sometime? It’d be good for the body and the mind. That sounds like a good plan. I’d be happy to join. I haven’t had much time to myself lately, and it would be nice to get out and about. If we go together, maybe we could even join the local choir again. I think they're looking for more members. It's a great way to meet people and keep the voice in shape. Hey, that’s a thought. I used to sing in a choir when I was working. It was a way to keep busy and meet people. I miss that a bit. But maybe now is the time to get back into it. I could do with some structure and a bit of social interaction. I think that's a fantastic idea. It’s one of those things you don’t realize how much you miss until you try to get back into it. And if we can all do it together, it’ll be even better. It’ll keep us active, keep us going, and maybe even help with the overall wellbeing. Exactly. And it doesn’t have to be too serious.

Okay, so I just got the Parent’s Evening feedback, and I think we need to talk about it. What did it say? Well, it’s mostly positive, but there were some concerns about maths. They said that both of you are struggling a bit with basic arithmetic and problem-solving. Yeah, I know. I just can’t get my head around fractions. I know, I’ve noticed that too. It’s not just about getting the right answer; it’s about understanding the steps. I think I just get confused when there are multiple steps. Like, if you have to add, then multiply, then divide – it feels like a maze. Yeah, and I think that’s why the teachers are worried. They mentioned that you need more practice with real-life examples, like dividing a pizza or splitting money. I mean, I can divide a pizza, but I can’t explain it to my teacher. That’s exactly what they said—your practical understanding is there, but your ability to articulate it in class is a bit limited. Should we get a tutor? I was thinking about that. But I also wanted to see if we could do some extra practice at home. Maybe we can do some online games or apps that make learning maths fun? Can we do it after dinner? I don’t want to do maths before my TV time. Well, we can definitely do it after dinner, but I think we should also talk about what’s going on in school. The teachers mentioned that you’re both very engaged in your other subjects, like English and science. Yeah, I love reading. They said I’ve got a really good imagination, and I can talk about characters in books for ages. That’s great. They even mentioned that you could maybe do a book report or something for World Book Day. I think that could help build your confidence in writing as well. What’s World Book Day? It’s an event in school where you get to read a book and maybe do a presentation or go to a special activity. I think the teachers are planning a reading challenge, and it’s a really good way to support your reading skills. That sounds fun. I might even read a book about a circus, like the one I saw on TV last week. That’s a great idea.

So, do you know what’s going on with Oisin? I’ve been trying to get him to help out at the curtain shop, but he keeps saying he’s too busy with his rugby training. Yeah, I know. He’s got this weird obsession with rugby now. Every time we mention it, he starts talking about how he’s going to be the best player in the county. Honestly, I think he’s gonna end up getting himself injured. [giggles] He’s just like his dad. You remember how he used to chase the football around the garden when he was little? It was like he couldn’t stop. Oh, he was a right little demon. My son, too. Still is, though. I think you just can’t stop the energy once it’s in the blood. I suppose that’s why we’re all trying to get him to work at the curtain shop. It’s not like he’s got any other prospects. His dad’s got the shop, and he’s got to learn something. Yeah, but I don’t think he takes it seriously. He says he’s going to be a rugby player, not some shop boy. Wait, isn’t he the one who’s been helping out with the birthday party? I thought he was going to be the treasurer. Oh, he is. He was meant to be in charge of the money, but he keeps asking for more. I think he’s got a thing about numbers. He’s always counting things. I think he wants to be a money man. Maybe that’s why he’s so obsessed with rugby. It’s all about strategy, you know. It’s a shame he doesn’t take more interest in the school stuff. I remember when I was his age, I used to read for hours. I’d get so caught up in books. You know, I was thinking about his birthday party again. We need to get the invitations out soon. Yeah, we should. He’s got a lot of friends coming from the rugby team, and some of his cousins from London. I think it’s gonna be a big one. Oh, I’m excited! I get to open the presents, right? You’ll be the one who gets the biggest one, I’m sure. We’ll see. I think we’re all going to need to chip in.

So, do you know what’s the funniest word game you’ve ever played? I mean, like, the one where you have to come up with words that start with the same letter as the previous word, and it goes on forever? Oh, you mean  Boggle ? Or maybe  Taboo ? I’ve played both, but I think  Taboo  is more of a memory game. No, no, no, I think you’re talking about  Word Chain —the one where you just keep going with the last letter, and the goal is to not get stuck. Yeah, that’s it! I love that game. You know, like if the last word was "apple," the next word has to start with "e," and so on. It’s so much fun. I remember once we had a game that lasted for like 20 minutes, and we ended up with words like "elephant," "tangible," "garden," and then we were stuck on "n" for a while. That sounds like a real challenge. I’ve tried that before, but I always get stuck on certain letters. For instance, if you end on a letter like "x" or "z," it’s really hard to come up with a new word. Yeah, and sometimes the words you come up with are just random and don’t even make sense. Like once I had to say "quilt," and then the next word had to start with "t," and I thought, "Okay, what’s a word that starts with 't' and comes after 'quilt'?" And then I said, "tiger," and then "geranium," and the next one had to start with "n." I couldn’t think of anything. That’s the classic! I remember the time we had to do that at a party. Someone started with "door," and then we went through "ordeal," "deal," "ally," "lyric," "ricotta," "taco," "ocelot," "tornado," "ornado," and then we were stuck. That's brilliant. I think the key is to think fast and not get too caught up on the rules. It's more about the fun than winning. Exactly. And it's amazing how sometimes the weirdest words can come up. Like, I once had a game where someone said "kangaroo," and then the next person had to start with "o." And they said, "okay," and then I said, "okay, I'm out." Oh, that's a classic! I think we should try to make a game sometime, just for fun.

So, do you remember that time we tried to sleep in the back of the van for the whole night? We were supposed to be doing some work, but we just ended up napping for like eight hours straight. Oh yeah! That was the time we were supposed to be doing a night shift at the warehouse and we just... fell asleep. I think we were still in our clothes and everything. I remember waking up with this weird headache and thinking, “What the hell happened last night?” Then I saw the sun coming through the window and realized we’d literally been sleeping the whole time. It was so funny. I mean, we were both like, “We’re working, we’re working,” and then bam, we’re asleep. It’s like our bodies just decided to take over. And I think we even had a fight about who was more responsible for the mess we made when we woke up. I mean, we didn’t even know what time it was. It was like 9 in the morning and we were still in the van. Yeah, and we had to explain to our boss why we were late. He just laughed and said, “You two look like you’ve been through a war.” I think it was the best thing that ever happened to us. I know, right? It’s like we were just two kids again. All that arguing and everything, but in the end, we were just having fun. There’s something about that kind of chaos that makes you feel alive. Definitely. I think that’s why we’re still friends. We can argue and be stupid and still end up laughing about it later. Yeah, I think that’s what makes the best friendships. We can be silly and not care about anything else. Like that time we tried to take a selfie with the dog in the van and it ended up looking like we were trying to photograph a ghost. Oh man, I still have that photo on my phone. I tried to delete it, but I just couldn’t. It’s like a relic of our youth. I keep it too. It’s like a reminder of all the stupid things we did. You know, like the time we got locked out of the house and had to climb through the window. Oh, that was brutal.

So, do you think we've got a chance with the application? I mean, it's for that new community center in the east end, right? I think we do. The council has been pushing for more community spaces, especially since the recent report about the lack of facilities in that area. They’re probably looking for something like this to address the issue. Yeah, and they mentioned a planning committee meeting next week. I think that's when the details will be formally presented. But I still feel like we need to be careful with the structure. We don't want to overcomplicate it. Exactly. The key is to keep it simple but effective. I’ve been thinking about the layout. Maybe a central area for meetings, then separate rooms for workshops and classes. That way, it can serve multiple purposes. That makes sense. But I was wondering, should we include something like a small café or a community kitchen? It could help with funding and also make the space more accessible to local people. That’s a good point. The council might appreciate the added value. But we need to be realistic about the costs. A café would require more infrastructure and ongoing maintenance, which could be a barrier. True. Maybe we could start with the core facilities – the meeting room, a few activity spaces, and maybe a small kitchen. If the project goes well, we can expand later. It’s better to start small and build from there. Yeah, and we should also think about the surrounding area. It’s a bit of a neglected part of the city, so having a community space could be a real boost for the neighborhood. Exactly. I mean, it’s not just about the building. It’s about bringing people together. The planning committee is going to care about that. They’re not just looking for a space; they want something that benefits the local community. I agree. So maybe we should highlight that in our presentation. Emphasize the social impact, the potential for events, and how it can help bridge the gap between the community and local services. That sounds like a solid strategy. I think we should also consider how we’ll fund it. Grants, maybe some local sponsorships, or even a fundraiser. We can’t afford to go in without some financial backing. Right. I’ve already spoken to a few local businesses.

So, do you know what’s up with Mrs. Thompson? I swear she’s been acting weird since last week. Yeah, I noticed too. She’s been acting all secretive, like she’s hiding something. I overheard her talking to her daughter on the phone the other day, and she kept saying, “Don’t tell anyone.” Huh. What did she say? Maybe she’s in trouble? Or maybe she’s got a new boyfriend? No, I don’t think so. She said something about a “big change” in her life. I think it might be something to do with her property. She’s been asking about selling the house, and she keeps checking the estate agents’ website like it’s going to fall apart any second. That’s odd. I mean, I thought she was pretty set in her ways. She always said she’d never leave this house, no matter what. Yeah, I know. And I think it’s got something to do with the new development down the road. I heard the council is planning to build a big shopping centre there, and she’s worried it’s going to ruin the area. But I also think she’s just trying to make something out of it. Maybe she’s thinking of selling and moving somewhere else? I mean, she’s getting on a bit, and the house is getting a bit run down. I don’t know. She might be, but I also wonder if it’s just her being dramatic. I mean, she’s always been like that. Remember when she had that massive argument with the postman last year over a late delivery? I still get a laugh out of it about that. Yeah, but she’s different now. It’s like she’s been going through something. I mean, she even started complaining about the garden last week—said she found a dead bird in the flower beds. I thought she was joking, but she actually looked really upset about it. Maybe it’s something else. You know, she’s been acting more anxious lately. Maybe she’s having trouble with her health? Or maybe she’s just been stressed with work? I don’t know. I suppose we’ll find out soon enough. But I think it’s best not to push her. You know, some people just need space to sort things out.

So, do you think we should do the washing up tonight or do you wanna wait for tomorrow? Well, I was just about to say, I don’t mind doing it, but I think we should do it tonight. We’ve had the TV on for ages, and I’d rather not leave it for tomorrow. Yeah, I agree. I reckon it’s about time we sorted it out. I was gonna do it anyway, so this way we can both watch a bit more of this show. Oh, I know, this show is so good. I’ve been watching it for like three episodes now. It’s like a mix of crime and drama, which I love. It’s like  Line of Duty  but with more... eccentric characters. Yeah, I watched the first episode, and I thought it was pretty good. Although, I was a bit confused at first. I mean, the dialogue is so fast, and the characters are all over the place. But I guess that’s part of the charm. Exactly. I thought the same thing. It’s a bit like NLP—everyone’s using different words to say the same thing. I mean, not literally, but there’s something about how they speak that’s really unique. It’s like they’re all trying to one-up each other, and it’s hilarious. Yeah, and don’t get me started on the car boot sales. Last weekend, I saw one where they had this old camera that looked like it belonged in a museum. And the guy just handed it over for €20. I thought it was a joke. That’s the thing with car boot sales, right? You never know what you’ll find. I mean, the other day I bought a vintage frying pan for like a fiver. It’s barely used, and it’s got this amazing patina on it. I’m saving it for my cooking class next week. Cooking class? Oh, you mentioned that before. When are you starting that again? Next week, actually. I’m doing it through a local community center. It’s a new initiative for people with dyslexia. I think it’s a great idea. It helps people feel more confident in the kitchen, and it’s a safe space to make mistakes. That’s really cool. I mean, I know how hard it can be to follow recipes when you have dyslexia.

So, do you know what’s been going on with the weather lately? I swear it’s been like a rollercoaster. One day it’s pouring buckets, the next it’s sunny and warm. It’s a bit of a headache when you’re trying to plan a weekend. Yeah, I know what you mean. I’ve been trying to decide whether to take the kids to the park or not. One minute I think it’s going to be perfect, and the next I’m checking the forecast again, wondering if it’s worth it. I’ve had the same problem. I even tried to use one of those weather apps, but honestly, it’s like they’re just guessing. One day it says 60% chance of rain, and then the next day it’s just sunshine. I’ve started to lose faith in them. I’ve had that too, but I’ve found a new app called Weather++ that’s pretty accurate. It actually gives you a week ahead, so you can plan ahead without second-guessing. I’ve been using it for a few weeks now and it’s been pretty reliable. I’m still with the default one on my phone, though. I’ve heard so many stories about people getting caught in the rain because they trusted the wrong app. I’m not taking any chances. I’ll just wait until the last minute and see what it does. Fair enough. I’ve heard that one too. Still, I’d say the worst part is not knowing what to wear. If you pack for a sunny day, you end up soaked, and if you pack for a rainy day, you end up sweating under a pile of layers. I know exactly what you mean. I had a meeting last week where I was wearing a light jacket, only for it to start drizzling. I felt like a fool. At least I had an umbrella, but that made me look like a tourist. That’s true. I remember one time I was at a café and there was a girl sitting next to me with an umbrella. She looked like she was ready to jump out of it. I felt bad for her because clearly, the weather had the best of her. You know, I think the real problem is that we’re all so used to relying on technology for everything, and when it lets us down, it’s like a small betrayal.

So, do you remember when we first moved to the area in the 1960s? I couldn’t believe how different it was from where I came from. I mean, I was a young teacher then, just fresh out of college, and the place felt like a whole new world. I remember that too, old friend. It was the same for me. I had just finished my training and came here for an interview to be a teacher. I got the job, but I was terrified. I didn’t know a soul and the houses were so different from what I was used to. Oh, I had even more of a struggle. I was applying to be a university lecturer, and I had to move to Manchester for that. I remember the first time I tried to find somewhere to live. You had to go through these little flats, and I ended up renting a place that looked like it had been through a war. The walls were peeling, and the floorboards creaked like it was about to fall apart. That sounds like nothing compared to what I went through. I came here for a dental course, and I had to find somewhere to live. I ended up in a place that only had a single bed and a tiny kitchen. I remember when I got home from my first day at the university, I was so tired, I just collapsed on the floor. I didn’t even have enough room to lie down. You were a dentist, right? I remember you telling us about that postgraduate course you did in Athens. It must have been a wild experience. Oh, it was! I was going there for a university course when the day of the dictatorship started. I remember walking into the classroom, and the professor just said, “Alright, everyone, listen up.” That was it. We were told to stay quiet, and we couldn’t even talk. It was like the whole country had gone on hold. Wow, that’s a story. I was in college in the 60s too, and I remember the time change when we went over to America for a study trip. I was so confused. I thought the clocks had gone backward, and I ended up calling my mum saying, “Mum, the clocks are goin’ the wrong way!” She just laughed and said, “No, love, it’s just the time difference.”

Well, it’s a lovely place, isn’t it? Taunton – I mean, it’s got that old-world charm, don’t you think? I’ve lived in Somerset all my life, so I know the area well. Though honestly, I’ve never been to Taunton myself. Just heard about it on the radio. Oh, really? I grew up in Sydney, so I don’t know much about England, but I’ve always been curious. I’ve heard Taunton is quite a place. What do you do now? You said you’re retired? Yes, I am. I was an artist and also ran an antique gallery for years. I had a little shop in Frome, actually. It was called  The Somerset Gallery . I sold all sorts – paintings, old furniture, things like that. Made a bit of a living, even if it wasn’t the most stable. And I still do a bit of painting in my spare time. That sounds fascinating! I used to work as a speech and language therapist. I worked with children, mostly. I loved it, but after retiring, I’ve been trying to find something new. I’ve taken up pottery – it’s a bit of a change of pace, but it’s quite calming, actually. Oh, pottery! I’ve always admired that. I used to have a friend who was a potter in the village. He made the most beautiful mugs and vases. He’d sell them at the local market. I think he’s still around, though I haven’t seen him in a while. That’s lovely. I’d love to try it – I’ve always been fascinated by the way people can make such beautiful things with their hands. But I still find it hard to let go of my old routine. It’s been years since I left the job, and I still feel like I need to ‘be useful’. I can relate to that. I used to feel the same way. But being retired has given me time to reflect. I’ve always been curious about the world, and I’ve travelled quite a bit – to places like Wales, Scotland, even parts of the Mediterranean. It’s been a way of keeping the mind active. That’s amazing. I’ve never really had the chance to travel – at least not in the way you did. I was always too busy with work.

So, do you think you're going to get your tattoo done before Christmas? Honestly, I’ve been thinking about it for weeks now. I’ve got this design I really like, but I’m just not sure if I’m ready. I mean, it’s not like I’m gonna regret it, right? No, I think once you decide, you just have to go for it. I got mine done last summer, and I don’t regret it at all. It’s a small little symbol of my journey through uni. Yeah, I guess. I just worry about the pain, honestly. I’ve never had anything done before. [enters the kitchen, holding a bag of decorations] Oi, you two, I’m back! I got the lights and the candy canes. Think we’re all set for Christmas now. You’re a lifesaver, Sam. I was just about to ask if we had the decorations. Don’t worry, I’ve got everything. The café’s been getting a bit quiet lately, so I figured I might as well get the festive spirit going early. Speaking of the café… are you still doing the Christmas pudding thing? Oh yeah, definitely. I’ve got a new recipe this year, something with a bit of brandy and a twist. You’ll love it. That sounds amazing. I’ve been craving something sweet and rich all week. I’ve been thinking about making some Christmas cookies too. I got this new chocolate melting stuff from the shop – it’s like a dream. Oh, you’ll have to bring some over. I’m hosting a little get-together next week with the other café owners. It’ll be like a mini Christmas market in the café. That sounds like a great idea. I’ll bring the cookies, and maybe some of my homemade trifle too. Trifle? I could get used to hearing you talk about trifle all the time. It’s the best thing ever. My mum taught me how to make it, and it’s just the perfect way to go out of my comfort zone in the kitchen. I’m sure you’ll be the star of the show. Although, I might have to steal some of your trifle for the café. Only if you promise to share the chocolate sauce with me. Deal. But honestly, I think you should get that tattoo done.

So, do you think I should go to Oxford or stay in Cambridge? Well, it depends on what you're looking for. Oxford is more traditional, I suppose. But Cambridge has its own charm, don’t you think? Yeah, I guess. But I’ve heard that Oxford is harder to get into, especially if you’re not from a big school. It is, but that’s not necessarily a bad thing. It just means you’ll have to work harder, which is a good thing. But are you even sure what you want to study? I’m still not entirely sure. I’m thinking about literature, maybe postcolonial studies. But I don’t want to be stuck in a city that’s too big. That’s understandable. I mean, I grew up in London, and I can tell you, it’s overwhelming. But sometimes the big cities offer more opportunities. Do you think you’d be comfortable in London? I don’t know, Mum. I mean, I like the idea of being near family, but I also feel like I need to move out and be on my own. You know, to figure things out. I get that. But you’re not alone in that. I left home when I was your age too, and I didn’t think I was ready, either. But sometimes you just have to take the plunge and see where it takes you. What do you think about me staying in Cambridge then? I mean, I know it’s not as glamorous as Oxford, but it’s familiar. I think it’s a good idea. You can take your time, explore your options, and maybe even switch to another course if you need to. But I do hope you take this opportunity to grow. Life doesn’t wait for you, you know. Yeah, I know. I just… I don’t want to make the wrong choice. I understand. But trust yourself. You’ve always been pretty clear about what you want. If you’re not sure yet, that’s okay too. Just don’t let fear keep you from trying. Thanks, Mum. I’ll think about it. And if you ever need advice, you know where to find me. I’ll always be here for you, no matter where you go. I know. And I’ll be back to visit soon, I promise. That’s all I need to hear.

So, do you know what’s going on with the alumni day? I’ve been meaning to ask someone about it. Oh yeah, I’m here for that! It’s such a great chance to reconnect with old friends and catch up on what everyone’s been up to. Yes, I’ve been here a few times. It’s always good to see people from the old days. Though I must say, it’s quite surprising to see how much the place has changed since I was a student. Really? I mean, Cambridge has always had a kind of timeless feel to it, hasn’t it? Oh, it does, but the people are always changing. I remember when I was a lecturer here, back in the late 70s, the atmosphere was very different. I’ve been thinking about traveling a lot lately, especially to the Middle East. I’ve always been fascinated by the region’s history and culture. That’s a great plan. I’ve been to Jordan and Syria a few times. I even did some work with an archaeological team excavating some ancient villages. It was fascinating. That sounds incredible. I’ve always been interested in archaeology, but I never thought I’d get the chance to be involved in anything like that. I mean, I’m more into languages than digging up old sites. Well, you never know. You could always go into fieldwork with your language studies. I did some work with a group looking at ancient scripts in the Levant. It combined language and history in a really meaningful way. That does sound like a great combination. I’ve been reading a lot about Arabic culture and history lately. I think I’d love to study Arabic more deeply, maybe even take a trip to study in Cairo. That sounds like a dream. I’ve been thinking about learning Chinese for a while now. It’s such a complex language, and I think it’s one of the most important languages to know these days. Absolutely. Chinese is an essential language for anyone interested in global affairs. I always found the structure of Chinese fascinating, especially the tonal system. Yeah, I’ve been trying to pick up some basic phrases. It’s tough, but I think it’s worth it. I’d love to be able to speak it fluently. I agree. It’s not just about the language itself, but also the culture and history that come with it.

So, do you think the way young people are educated these days is actually helping them out in the real world? I mean, I've got friends who are doing degrees and then can't even write a proper CV. It's like they're learning things they'll never use. Honestly, I think it's all about the  class  system, you know? Like, if you come from a privileged background, you’ve got all these connections and your parents know people in the right places. Whereas someone like me, growing up in a working-class family, got into baking through sheer hard work and luck. You don’t get that kind of support from school. Yeah, and I’ve seen it firsthand with my café. My staff are all young people with degrees, and they can’t even handle basic accounting or customer service. It’s like they’ve been taught to think in theory but not in practice. I mean, I know it’s a different world now, but still... I don’t know. I agree, but I think it's not just the education system—it’s the way society is structured. If someone has dyslexia, they might not be able to keep up with the same academic pace as others. I had a friend at university who was dyslexic and was constantly told “just try harder.” But it's not that simple, you know? Exactly. I mean, don’t get me wrong—education’s important, but if you don’t have the right tools or support, it can be a massive barrier. And not everyone has the same opportunities. I had a lecturer once who said, “If you can’t handle the pressure, you shouldn’t be in this field.” But what about people who are actually capable? They’re just not being given the chance to show it. I think part of the problem is the perception of what it means to be “successful.” Like, everyone’s chasing that “dream job” in London or a big city, but maybe they don’t consider other paths. Like, I’ve always loved baking, and I chose that over a nine-to-five job. I know people say it’s not as “respectable,” but it works for me. That’s true, but I think it’s also the way the education system is set up. If you’re not going to go to university, you’re automatically seen as less valuable.

So, do you think we should be making any changes to our health insurance? I mean, with the new government policies, it's getting more complicated. I know, I've been thinking about that too. It feels like every time we try to plan something, there's another policy change that messes it up. I just don't know if it's worth the hassle. Yeah, I feel that way too. But I think we should at least check what's covered. It's not like we're in the best shape financially, so we need to be careful. Absolutely. I was actually thinking about it last night. I remember reading something about the NHS waiting times increasing again. It’s like they don't care if people are in pain or not. That’s terrible. I can’t imagine having to wait months for something that’s so basic. I’ve got this back injury that’s been bothering me for a while now, and I’m just waiting to see the GP. I know, and the GP just said they can’t see you for a few weeks. What are we supposed to do? I mean, we’re not even in the best place financially, and now we’re having to deal with this mess. It’s so frustrating. I remember when we first got married, everything was so much simpler. There weren’t these endless hoops to jump through to get basic healthcare. Yeah, I remember that too. We never thought this would be the case. I mean, we’re in a country that’s supposed to be one of the best, and now it feels like we’re being left in the lurch. I know, and then there’s the whole finance thing. With the interest rates going up, it’s like we’re being hit from all sides. I barely have time to breathe, let alone plan for the future. I feel you. I’ve been trying to save up for a new laptop for work, but every time I think I’ve got some money saved, something comes up. It’s such a tightrope to walk. I know. It’s just so easy to feel overwhelmed. I think we need to start setting some boundaries. I mean, we can’t keep worrying about everything all the time. True. I think we need to focus on what we can control, rather than getting caught up in all the chaos.

Well, I've just made some roast potatoes and a bit of gravy. I thought it would be nice to have a proper lunch today, especially with the weather being so miserable outside. That sounds lovely, thank you. I’m really glad you decided to cook today. I was just about to mention that I’ve been thinking about how much I miss the simple things—like sitting down for a proper meal with a bit of chat. Yeah, I know what you mean. I used to love cooking for the family when we were all living together. Those days are a bit of a distant memory now, though. It’s been a while since we’ve had a real family meal like this. Oh, it’s been too long, I agree. I think we should start a tradition of having lunch together every Sunday, like we used to when the kids were younger. It’d be a nice way to catch up and remember old times. That sounds like a great idea. And it would give us a chance to talk about the old days. I was just thinking about the time when we all used to go on holiday every year. I remember one particular trip to the Lake District. It was the first time I tried hiking properly, and I nearly got lost! You were so proud of yourself when you got back, weren’t you? You were sure you’d found a new path that no one else had taken. You even wrote a little poem about it. Oh yes, that was one of the more memorable moments. I still have that poem tucked away in an old notebook. It’s a bit of a treasure. But I suppose it’s all part of the fun of growing up and living through those experiences. I think the beauty of family is that we can all share these stories and memories. It’s like a time capsule of our lives. I was just thinking, too, about the holidays we used to have at my mum’s. She always made the most amazing Christmas cakes. I still remember the smell of that cake, even when I was a child. Oh, I’ve had that same cake with my family a couple of times. It’s such a comforting thing, isn’t it? The smell and the taste, it always brings back so many memories.

So, do you know what games you're playing with the little one, Lenny? Yeah, I've been playing with him with some soft toys. He loves them. Oh, soft toys? Are they the ones with the squeaky noises? Yeah, exactly. He likes to shake them and make the squeaky sounds. That’s great. I remember when I was a kid, I used to love those toys too. They were like little friends. Yeah, they're so easy to play with. You don’t need any special skills. I suppose they’re perfect for a toddler. It’s like a sensory experience, isn’t it? Absolutely. They help with motor skills and also provide comfort. I know. It’s like he’s learning to interact with the world through those toys. That’s so important. I remember when my brother was little, he used to have a teddy bear that he never left. Yeah, that’s a common thing. I think we all have that kind of early attachment. He also likes to play with the ones that have little buttons or things to press. Oh, I like that. It’s interactive. It keeps his attention for longer. Definitely. It’s a great way to keep him engaged and entertained. I also got him a few soft animals. He likes to push them around and make them roll. That’s a nice way to encourage movement. I think it’s important to keep the toys soft to avoid any injuries, especially for a toddler like him. Yeah, I’ve made sure all the toys are safe and have no sharp edges. Good. I remember when my nephew was younger, there was a toy that was too hard and he ended up with a bruise. That’s a good reminder. Safety first, especially with young kids. I’ve also been reading some articles about how soft toys can help with language development too. That’s interesting. I didn’t know that. Maybe I should look into that. Yeah, I think it’s all about providing a safe and stimulating environment for the toddler to grow and learn. I think we’re doing a great job. He’s always smiling and seems so happy. That’s the main thing. We just want him to have fun and feel safe. Right. And we’re all in this together, so it’s a team effort.

Right, right, we've got to get the car serviced before Christmas. I was just thinking, it's been a while since we had it checked. Yeah, I know. I saw a sign on the side of the road saying “Free Car Service” at the motor shop down by the village. I thought we could take advantage of that. That sounds good. But have you got a spare wheel? I mean, if the car breaks down on the way to the Christmas dinner, it’s going to be a nightmare. Oh, don’t be so dramatic. We’ve got a spare wheel, and even if it does go, we can walk to the pub and have a few drinks. It’s not like we’re going all the way to London or something. Dad, you can’t just walk to the pub. It’s like three miles away! Well, it’s not that far if you’ve got a good pair of boots on, and the weather’s nice, which it’s always been this time of year. Or at least, it should be. Yeah, but the last time we did that, we got stuck in the rain for two hours. You were in a proper rage, Dad. I remember you shouting at the car like it was alive. Oh, I remember that. You thought the engine was trying to sabotage you somehow. You even started trying to talk to it like it was your friend. That was the day we also got a flat tyre on the way back. I had to change it with a kid who was just learning how to do it. Made a right mess of it, too. Oh, don’t start. You were the one who said, “It’s just a tyre, love. Let’s get it done and over with.” And now we’re all here, and you’ve got a big mark on your hand from the spare wheel. And the one time you tried to give it a name, it was called “Bert.” You said it was “never going to let us down.” Yeah, and it didn’t. It just took the whole night to get us home. I think the car got the better of us that day. It’s like it was trying to teach us a lesson, or something. Well, it’s what we all need. A lesson. Especially after the Christmas dinner last year, where we ended up with a burnt pie because the oven was broken.

So, do you know what’s on for the weekend, Lottie? I was just thinking about what we could do. You know, after all that work week. Honestly, I’d just like to lie in bed and not do anything. I’ve been working on a big project at the office, and I’m absolutely knackered. But I suppose I should do something fun. Well, I was thinking we could go to that new café in Canterbury. I heard they’ve got some amazing coffee and a nice outdoor seating area. It’s been ages since we went out. Yeah, but I’ve heard they’ve been getting a lot of complaints about the food. People say it’s not up to scratch. Although, I suppose you can’t really complain about the view, can you? I’d rather not go somewhere where the food is questionable, to be honest. I’d rather just have a takeaway and watch a film. You know, like we used to do when we were younger. Yeah, I know. But we’ve got to try and do something, otherwise we’ll just end up staying in every weekend. It’s not healthy, is it? We need to get out and about. I’m not sure. I mean, I miss the days when we could just go out and have fun without having to worry about the weather or the cost. These days, everything costs something. Even a cup of coffee at that café, I heard, was like £4. That’s not even fair. I mean, I buy a coffee for £2.50 and that’s being expensive. If I had to pay £4 for a coffee, I would just skip it altogether. I’m not even joking. I know what you mean. But you know what’s even more worrying? The cost of living in general. My sister’s got a mortgage and she’s struggling to make ends meet. I just feel like everything’s getting more expensive. It’s like the government’s trying to make us all poor. Yeah, and I know what you mean. Even my flatmates are talking about it. We’ve got to be careful with our money these days. I’ve even cut down on my coffee because I can’t afford to buy it every day. I know. I’ve been trying to save up for a big birthday present for my mum.

I don’t know, I just feel like things have changed so much. I remember when we used to go to the park and the kids would play outside all day, and now it’s all screens and everything. Yeah, I know what you mean. It’s like the world’s gone past us, isn’t it? I used to think the internet was just a thing for the young, but now I’ve got to use it to order groceries and pay bills. It’s all about convenience, really. You don’t even have to leave the house anymore. I mean, I still prefer going to the shop, but I can’t deny it’s easier to order online and have it delivered. That’s the thing, isn’t it? It’s just life moving on. I remember when we had to wait for the postman every day. Now, it’s all instant. You can get anything in a matter of hours. But what about the social part of it? I mean, do you think we’re losing something? I still miss the days when we’d have a chat with our neighbors, or meet up with friends for a cup of tea. Now, people are too busy or too glued to their phones. I know, it’s sad. I used to love the church, and the sense of community there. These days, I’m not sure if people even go. It’s like the world’s turned its back on tradition. Oh, I still go to church. It’s good to have that connection. But I admit, the service is a bit different these days. The music’s changed, the preaching’s more political, and I don’t know about the new hymns. I can see that. I think some people like it that way, but I prefer the old school stuff. I still remember the hymns from when I was a kid. They had a certain feel to them. I was thinking about that the other day. I was walking past the church, and I remembered how we used to have a big feast every Christmas. Now, it’s just a few people turning up, and the food’s not as good. Maybe it’s because people have more on their plate now. With all the work and responsibilities, I don’t think they have the time anymore.

So, do you know what’s on tonight? I’ve been meaning to catch that new film with the guy who played the robot in  Iron Man —he’s in this one called  The Last Star . I heard it’s got some serious action and the plot’s not too bad. Yeah, I saw the trailer. It looks intense. I actually saw the first one last week— The Last Star: Origins —and it was pretty good. I mean, it’s not  Star Wars , but it’s got that same kind of epic feel. Although, honestly, I don’t know why they’re calling it  The Last Star  if there’s still a whole galaxy to explore. Yeah, that’s a bit confusing. But I guess it’s just a marketing thing. I’m just hoping this one doesn’t drag. I’ve been trying to get into more movies lately, but with work and everything, it’s been hard to find time. Plus, I’m not really into the sci-fi genre unless it’s got explosions and cool spaceships. I can relate. I do love the explosions, though. Honestly, I think I’m more into the action sequences than the actual story. But then again, I’m not watching it for the plot. I’m just here for the visuals and the soundtrack. Plus, I’ve got a bit of a thing for the soundtrack of  The Last Star —it’s got that really cool orchestral feel. Oh, I love that. The music in that first movie was amazing. I remember hearing it on the radio and just thinking, “That’s the kind of vibe I want in my life.” Although, I guess I’m not the most serious about movies. I mean, I still remember the time I tried watching  The Godfather  and ended up crying because of that one scene with the horse. You’re not the only one. I remember when I first watched  The Godfather —I was 16 and had no idea what was going on. I just thought it was a really dramatic movie with a lot of swearing and cool suits. Then, one day, I watched it again and realized what was happening. I was so emotional, I cried for like 20 minutes. I bet you were. I had that same experience with  The Lion King . I watched it when I was 10, and then again when I was 20.

So, do you know what’s going on with the Scottish referendum? I’ve been trying to keep up with it, but it’s all a bit confusing. Yeah, I know. It’s a big deal, isn’t it? I mean, I’ve heard people talking about it at school. They say it’s about whether Scotland should leave the UK and become its own country. Right. And I think it’s coming up soon, isn’t it? I remember hearing something about a vote in the next few months. Yeah, I think it’s supposed to be in the autumn. I’m not sure exactly when, though. I think it’s the same way as other elections, like the local ones, but bigger. Yeah, I guess. But I’m not sure what the arguments are. I mean, I know some people say Scotland is better off on its own, but I don’t really understand why. It’s still part of the UK, isn’t it? Well, some people say the UK government isn’t giving Scotland enough money or power. Like, maybe they want more say in things like taxes and laws. And also, they’re worried about the economy. I think there was something about oil and gas in Scotland too, like they want to control that. Oh, right. I remember hearing something about that. So, if Scotland becomes its own country, it would be like a separate nation, but still part of the European Union, I suppose? I think so. Or maybe they’d have to negotiate that. Some people think it would be hard, especially because the UK is part of the EU right now. But others say it’s about freedom and identity. Interesting. I guess it’s a big decision for the people of Scotland. I wonder how it will affect the rest of the UK too. I mean, if they do leave, it could change a lot of things. Yeah, I suppose. And it’s not just about money or politics, it’s also about culture and history. A lot of people in Scotland feel they have their own identity, separate from England. That makes sense. I mean, I know the UK is made up of different countries, like Wales and Northern Ireland too. I wonder if they’re thinking about that as well. I don’t know. I think the Scottish referendum is getting a lot of attention, though.

I swear, I can't understand a word he's saying. It’s like he's talking in code or something. Yeah, I know, isn’t it? I think it’s because he's from Liverpool, so his accent is so thick, even for a TV show. It’s like he’s on a different planet. I get it. I mean, I’ve heard that sort of accent before, but I think he's doing this on purpose, like, making it even more exaggerated. It’s like he’s trying to be the most Yorkshire of them all, but he's from Liverpool. Oh, come on, he’s not from Yorkshire. He’s from Liverpool. That’s like saying the Queen is from Manchester. It’s just not right. Yeah, I mean, I can barely understand him without the subtitles. But then again, he’s got that weird way of speaking, like he’s always dropping words. "I’ve got a bit of a cold, so I'm not feeling too good today." Wait, what? Did he say that or was I just imagining it? Exactly! I think that's called elision. Like, when people drop sounds or syllables in their speech. It’s super common in Northern accents, but I still can’t get it. I mean, I know what elision is, but I can’t hear it in real life. You know what I think? I think it's not just elision—it's like full-on phonetic warfare. Like, he's trying to sound like he's from the North, but he's from the North West. It’s confusing. Yeah, and it’s not about just the accent. It's about the way he uses words. Like, he says "cider" like it's "cider" but with a weird twist. Maybe he’s trying to sound like he's from the North, even though he's not. It’s so unfair. I think the reason he does it is because he’s on TV, and he wants to be relatable. He’s doing it to make people think he’s a real working-class guy. But he's not. He's just a TV presenter. That's probably it. But I still can't get over how much he drops his "th" sounds. It’s like he’s talking to himself or something. It’s like he’s in a different dimension.

I can't believe the amount of money they're spending on that striker. I mean, he's only been on the team for a couple of months and already they're talking about signing him for like, double what he was worth. I know, it’s such a shame. But maybe it’s because he’s from Manchester? I mean, they always seem to overpay for players from the North. It’s like they think they’re some kind of special breed. Yeah, I guess, but even so, why not just watch the games and see how he performs? I mean, he’s not even been to the Champions League yet. I can’t see how they’re just throwing money around like that. I get that, but you know how it is. Once you get a player who’s got a bit of hype around him, the club just goes all in. They don’t want to miss out on the chance to be seen as the big club in the league. It’s all about branding and image, really. I suppose. But I still think it’s a bit strange, especially with the current financial situation. I mean, with all the clubs struggling with debt and everything, you’d think they’d be more careful with their transfers. You’re not wrong. But then again, the Premier League is such a different beast now. It’s not just about winning anymore, it’s about selling tickets, selling merchandise, and having a brand. It’s all business. I guess. But I can’t help but feel like we’re losing sight of the actual game. I mean, I love football, but I also love watching the talent come through. You know, the raw, young players who play with heart and skill, not just money. True. I mean, that’s why I still love watching the younger teams, the ones that come from the academy. They’re the ones who actually make the game fun. The players with the hunger. You know, the ones who don’t have millions behind them but still play with passion. Yeah, exactly. I think that’s what makes the game special. It’s not just about the big names and the money. It’s about the love of the game, the passion, the stories. You know, like the ones about players who started in the local league and worked their way up.

So, do you remember The Bee Movie? You know, that one where the bees are trying to save the world? Oh yeah, I remember that! I think it was the one with the little bee who wanted to be a king, right? Yeah, I think that’s the one. But I don’t think the bees really wanted to be kings. They were just trying to save their hive. Exactly! And it was funny because they thought the queen was like the boss, but in the end, they realized that working together was better than having one ruler. That’s so true. I think that’s the real message of the movie. You don’t need to be a king or a queen to make a difference. I guess that’s why I always say, if you want to be a king, just be a good friend. You don’t need a crown to be respected. Exactly! And speaking of being respected, have you seen those videos about people trying to get into the Royal Palaces? Like, you know, paying a fortune just to walk through the gates? Oh yeah, I’ve seen those. It’s so weird how people are willing to pay so much just to see the same old rooms. I mean, wouldn’t it be better to just visit the palace gardens for free? Maybe, but I think some people just like the idea of being in the same space as royalty. Like, even if it’s just a photo op. Yeah, and then there’s the whole debate about being a republic versus a monarchy. Do you think the UK should become a republic? I mean, the Queen is pretty old now. I think it’s time for her to step down. But I don’t think we should just throw out the monarchy entirely. Maybe just make it symbolic. Yeah, I think that’s the way to go. Like, the Queen could still be a symbol of unity, but not the head of state. That makes sense. I think a lot of people are just tired of the whole royal family drama. But I do love the way they sometimes support charities and go to events. They do have their good sides. Yeah, and they’re not all about the money either. Some of them really care about helping people. Like the Queen’s charities, right?

So, do you know, I was just thinking about how much easier everything was back in the day when we didn’t have to worry about all this technology and stuff. Just go out, throw a stick, and a dog would follow you. No need for a GPS or anything. Oh, I remember that! I used to take my dog out every morning and just let him roam. It was like a ritual. But now, with all these rules about dog walking and picking up after them, it's just not the same. Especially with the new council rules. Yeah, and with all the different breeds now, it's like you can't even go out without someone asking you what kind of dog you have. It’s like a full-time job just to walk the dog these days. I know, I’ve had to do that. My dog’s a labrador, and every time I take him out, someone always asks if he’s got any allergies or if he’s been vaccinated. It’s like we’re all in some kind of strange health and safety environment. I know, and it’s not just dogs. I went to the tip the other week, and the guy there was telling me how they’ve got this new system where you have to scan your bin every time. It’s just another thing to complain about. That’s not even the worst. I was telling my mum the other day about this new app that tells you what’s in your recycling and what you can throw away. It’s so detailed, you can’t even throw out a banana peel without checking what you’re allowed to. It’s like they’re trying to make us all feel guilty for not being perfect. I mean, I don’t even know what the different categories are. I just throw everything into the bin and hope for the best. That’s probably the safest way. But I tried using the app once, and I thought I was doing the right thing, but the bin got sent to the wrong place. I had to call them up and explain that I was just trying to be responsible. It’s ridiculous. I think the real issue is that the government keeps trying to make things more complicated. You know, it’s like the more they try to help us, the more problems they create.

So, do you know what’s happening with the museum thing? I was thinking maybe we could go together this weekend. Yeah, I was just thinking about that! I saw an article about a new exhibition opening in the Liverpool Museum. It’s about the history of the city, which sounds really interesting. That’d be cool. I’ve been meaning to check it out for a while. I remember when I was a student, I used to go there all the time. The old exhibits were so cool, you know? Yeah, I remember when we first moved in, you were always like, “Let’s go to the museum!” I think we went there at least six times in the first month. Oh, you remember that? It was ridiculous. I think I got tired of walking around the place, but it was good for the soul, you know? Definitely. Anyway, if we go, are you alright with parking? I saw the car park is a bit of a nightmare, especially on weekends. Yeah, I know. I’ve got a friend who lives nearby, and I think he puts his car in their garage. Maybe I can borrow it. Or we could take the tram? I remember it’s only like a 10-minute ride? That’d be better. I don’t like the idea of getting stuck in a queue for an hour just trying to park. Besides, the tram passes the city centre, so we could stop off for a quick coffee on the way. Sounds like a plan. Although, I need to check if I can get a weekend pass for the museum. I think it’s cheaper than buying tickets on the day. Yeah, that’s a good idea. I can look into that. Oh, and I was thinking about the housing thing too. Maybe we should start looking for a bigger place soon. Our current flat is getting too small for both of us, and the pets are starting to take over. Yeah, I’ve been thinking about that too. I know we’re not in a rush, but we should probably plan a little bit more. Especially with the Masters interview coming up. I can’t believe we've got to this point. That old cupboard’s been in the corner of the living room for years, and now we’re actually going to tidy it out. It’s a bit scary, isn’t it? But now that we are, it’s like we’re reconnecting with parts of our childhood. I feel emotional, to be honest. It’s a little sad that we’ve got so far, but also a bit nostalgic. I know. I can’t believe it’s been so long since we had those toys. I wonder if our kids would remember anything like that. Probably not.

I can't believe we've got a baby in the pram and we're walking through the park with mosquitoes buzzing around us like it's some kind of evil infestation. I know, I swear it's like they’re after us specifically. I’ve been swatting them all the way here and I still feel like I’ve got one on my neck. It’s not just you. Well, I've just marked a whole pile of maths papers, and I can tell you, it's been a real eye-opener. Some of the kids are so confused about basic algebra, it's ridiculous. Yeah, I heard about that. My maths teacher said the same thing. I don’t even know how they pass the exams sometimes. Oh, I had to do maths at school too. A lot worse than now, in my day. We had to do all the calculations by hand, no calculators. It was harder, but at least we knew how to do it properly. I remember being in the same class as you, dear. I used to help you with your homework. My wife still laughs when she remembers how I got so frustrated trying to teach you to do long division. I think it's because of all the technology now. Kids rely on calculators and apps to do everything. They don’t even know their multiplication tables by heart anymore. Yeah, and the way they're taught now is so different too. I mean, it's not like we used to have to memorise all the formulae. It was all about understanding the process, not just getting the right answer. That’s what I like about it. Back then, we had to understand the  why  behind the maths, not just the  how . It made us think, and that’s important. I suppose that’s why some people still get confused when they're older. They never really grasped the basics, so it's harder to pick it up again. Exactly. I’ve had a few students over the years who come back to do GCSEs after a long time. It’s always shocking how much they've forgotten. I know. I used to think I was pretty good at maths, but now I’m like, 'What’s a quadratic equation again?' Come on, you’re a grown man, not a child. You should be able to remember that! Well, I can’t say I’ve ever had to do much maths since I retired. I do the shopping and the budgeting, but I’m not too bad. I just need to add up the prices on the till, that’s all. That’s not hard. I suppose it’s the same thing as learning times tables. It’s just practice. Yeah, and if I keep on doing it, I’ll get better.

Alright, do you remember that time we watched  Peter Pan  on a rainy afternoon? It was like the first time I ever saw it, and I was so fascinated by the idea of Neverland. Yeah, I remember that! But I think you were more into  Pan  than  Peter Pan —the one with the pirate ship and all the adventure. Yeah, that was the one with the pirate ship, wasn’t it? My mum would laugh and say, “You’re not even allowed to be a grown-up yet!” She still says that! And she’s not even that old. I mean, she’s like, what, thirty? And she’s always telling us we’re too young to do things. Like, I tried to make a cake once when I was eight, and she said I was too young to bake. I was like, “I can do it!” And I did, but it looked like a disaster. I tried to cook a sandwich once. I put the bread in the toaster, and then I forgot about it. When I came back, it was burnt, and the toaster was smoking.

So, do you think we’ll get there in time for the flight? I was just checking the traffic, and it’s still a bit slow on the A38. I don’t want to be rushing through the airport like we were last time. I just want to have something to look forward to. Yeah, that’s why I’m trying to plan the house-warming party. My brother’s still in Taunton, and he’s got to drive all the way up here. That’s going to be a long drive for him. I remember when he used to come over for Christmas, it took him three hours just to get here.

Oh, do you know, I’ve been reading up on the ME event next year. It’s going to be a real big deal, isn’t it? I heard it’s all about women’s involvement in leadership and equality, which is really important. Yeah, I heard about that too. It’s a bit of a milestone, isn’t it? Aye, and I think it’s not just about education either. It’s about giving women more say in all areas of life. Like, for instance, in the workplace. I remember when I was working, you didn’t see many women in management. It was all blokes. Oh, I know. My husband always said that when he was younger, he didn’t think twice about it. But now, I think men are starting to see it as a good thing. It’s fairer for everyone, really. That’s true. I mean, I’m not saying that all men are the same, but I think the tide is turning. I mean, look at Margaret Thatcher, she was a trailblazer. It’s inspiring to see the progress. She was a real pioneer, no doubt about it. But I think we still have a long way to go. I mean, just think about the current state of things. There are still too many glass ceilings. Oh, I agree. But I think awareness is growing, and people are starting to understand the importance of equality. It’s not just about women—it’s about fairness for everyone. Exactly. And I think the ME event is a great opportunity to push that message forward. I hope it brings more attention to the issues that women still face. Yeah, and I think it’s also a good chance for women to share their experiences and support one another.

I mean, you’re not that old. You’ve got plenty of time to find something that fits. And I know you’re pretty handy with tools, and I think you could do something in the trades again. Yeah, I suppose. But I just worry about the interview part. I don’t know how to present myself anymore. I mean, I used to have that confidence, but now... I just feel like I’m not as capable as I used to be. I think you’re still capable, Tom. You just need to remind yourself of that. And maybe start small. Like, apply for some temp work or part-time jobs. That way, you can get back into the groove without the pressure of a full-time role. I guess that’s a good idea. I mean, I could always help out at the local community centre. They’ve been looking for someone to do some maintenance work. It’s not much, but it’s something. That sounds perfect. And it would give you a chance to meet people again, which is good for the social side. I know how much you miss being part of a group. Yeah, I do. I feel like I’ve been cutting myself off from friends and family. I just don’t know how to re-enter the world. It’s like I’m living in a bubble. You’re not alone in that. I know a few people who’ve been through similar things. It’s tough, but it gets easier. And you’re not going to find your way back unless you take the first step. I know. I just don’t know where to start. Maybe I should look into some job support services or something?

Alright lads, let's clear up the table. You two have been eating like you haven’t seen a meal in weeks. Yeah, sorry Mum. I was just thinking about the tennis match we watched yesterday. That’s fine, but you need to help out. You’re not a child anymore. She’s right, lads. You’re both in secondary school now. You should be contributing. I’m not contributing, I’m just trying to survive. That’s not the point. We all have to pitch in. You know what it’s like running a house, especially when you’ve got two teenage boys around. Yeah, well, you know, I’ve been thinking about Hitler’s speeches. They’re kinda interesting, like, how he used language to get people to follow him. You’ve been watching too much history, lad. You need to focus on your studies. I’m not interested in that, I’m more interested in Instagram. I’ve got like 200 followers now. That’s not the point of Instagram, is it? It’s about real life, not just likes and comments. I know, but it’s just how people communicate now. You know, with all the filters and stuff. I get that, but don’t let it distract you from your actual work. You’re in Year 11, you’ve got exams coming up. Yeah, but I already got my GCSE results. I’m just waiting to find out if I got into the college I applied for. That’s great, I’m proud of you. But you still need to help out around the house. You’re not a child anymore. I know, it’s just that I’ve got a lot on my mind. Like, I’ve been thinking about my girlfriend. She’s been on my mind a lot lately. Oh, so you’ve got a girlfriend now? That’s good news. Yeah, but it’s not like we’re dating properly yet. It’s just, you know, we’re friends with benefits. That’s not good, lad. You need to be careful. You don’t want to get your heart broken. I know, but it’s what we both want. We’ve been seeing each other for a few months now. I think it’s great that you’ve got someone. But you need to make sure you’re not treating her like a side project.

So, do you think we should get new furniture for the flat? I’ve been thinking it’s time to upgrade a bit, you know, with the kids starting to grow up and all. Yeah, I mean, it’s not like we’re in a bad situation, but the place is getting a bit worn out. I’d say it’s definitely time for a change. You know, I’ve been thinking too. I remember when I first got married, we had this old armchair that was practically a relic. It was so uncomfortable, but we kept it because we didn’t want to throw it out. It was like a family heirloom. Oh, I can imagine. You know, My mum still has that old rocking chair from when she was a girl. It’s got the most ridiculous springs, but it’s got character. I was just thinking about the tip last week, though. You know, the one with the guy in the van shouting, “We’re not here to help, we’re here to make money!” It was so ridiculous. Oh yes! That was a joke, wasn’t it? Like, “I don’t want to be on the tip, I want to be on the ladder!” I thought it was brilliant. Mate, I got a gift last Christmas from one of the neighbours. It was a tea set. I did not want it. You know what I did? I put it in the charity shop. They said it was in good condition. I said, “Yeah, just like I am.” That’s a good one. I remember being told once that if you don’t want it, you can give it to someone else. I thought, “How do I know they’ll want it?” That’s the thing, isn’t it? People just give stuff without thinking. I had a relative give me a whole set of cooking books. I haven’t opened them since 2012. Oh, I tried to return them. I went to the shop, and they said, “We can’t take it back.” I said, “I just want to give it away, not keep it.” But no, they said, “We can’t.” I was really upset. I think it’s better to just keep it, even if you don’t use it. You never know when your hobby might come back. Yeah, and then there’s the other thing—people think they know your life better than you do.

So, mum, I just wanted to check in with you about that redundancy thing at work. I know it's been a bit of a whirlwind lately, but I’m trying to figure out what the next steps are. Oh, I know, love. It's been so stressful. I’ve had meetings all week, and honestly, it’s been a bit of a rollercoaster. But I think I’ve got a handle on it now. They’re just trying to streamline things a bit, and I guess they’re looking to cut some roles. Yeah, I heard the school’s been doing a lot of restructuring. I’m just worried about how it’s going to affect your job security. Have you had any offers yet? Not yet, but I’m keeping my options open. I’ve been talking to a few people in the area, and I’m actually considering a move closer to the city. I heard there’s a new school opening up, and they’re looking for people with your experience.
